House again in Committee on Bill (No. 235) to provide for the construction of a National Transcontinental Railway.-The Prime Minister.
On section 7-Grand Trunk Railway Company may hold securities.

Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that the government is assuming a somewhat peculiar attitude in regard to this whole undertaking. The preamble of the Bill and the recital to the agreement both point to the fact that the intentions of the government in pressing this measure upon the House were to establish an all-Canadian route and to provide for the transportation of Canadian freight at Hon. Mr. FITZPATRICK.
as cheap rates as possible. Notwithstanding that fact, we had the spectacle yesterday of the government voting down all the stipulations suggested on this side of the House which were intended to prevent the diversion of traffic, and we had the spectacle, moreover, of the members of the government sitting 'Silently in their seats without saying a word after it had been pointed -out to them over and over again from this side of the House that the danger, as far as the diversion of traffic is concerned, was to be feared from the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and not from the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. Notwithstanding that, there was an absolute refusal from the treasury benches to impose on the Grand Trunk Railway Company a single one of the stipulations which are imposed on the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company by this contract. Not only was this the case, but the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) was put up by the government, in the first place, to answer the suggestions made on this side of the House, by a reference of matters to fifteen or twenty years ago. After that we had the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mi-. Charlton) put up to deliver speeches, covering, I suppose, an hour, or an hour and a half in all, in regard to grades which were absolutely irrelevant to the subject we were then discussing. We can only assume, under these circumstances, that it is the policy of my right hon. friend (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier), and of his government, to permit traffic to be diverted from Canadian routes, provided it is to be done by the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Otherwise, surely, there iis no reason for failing to impose upon that railway company some of the precautions which the government have thought wise to impose on the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. That is one aspect of the ease. Another aspect of the case is the one to which I am about to draw attention in connection with 'the amendment I have moved. I gave notice of a motion to this effect, as an amendment to section 7 of the Bill :
That section 7 he amended hy adding thereto the following -subsections :-
Notwithstanding anything in this Act, or in the said agrememt contained, His Majesty the King, -acting as aforesaid, shall not be hound or obliged to -perform, cary out or fulfil any of the covenants, conditions or stipulations in the said agreemnt contained on behalf of the Dominion of Canada unless and until the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall have subscribed for the common stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company payable in cash at par to the amount of not less than $24,300,000.
I understand that the hon. Minister of Justice is willing to accept that amendment, provided I strike out from it the words ' have subscribed for,' and insert in their stead the words 'shall acquire and

take,' and provided also that I shall strike out the words ' payable in cash at par.' I will read the amendment as it is suggested by the kon. Minister of Justice, because I will have to explain to the committee the reasons why I am unable to accept the amendment which is suggested by the government. The amendment as proposed by the bon. Minister of Justice is as follows :
That section 7 be amended by adding thereto the following subsections :-
(2) Notwithstanding anything in this Act or in the said agreement contained, His Majesty the King acting in respect of the government of Canada shall not he bound or obliged to perform, carry out or fulfil any of the covenants. undertakings, conditions or stipulations in the said agreement contained on behalf of His Majesty the King acting as aforesaid, unless and until the Grand Tramt 1 tailway Company of Canada shall acquire and take the common stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to the amount of not less than $24,900,000.
My proposal is that the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall subscribe for the stock at par, and shall incur all liabilities incident to such subscription, hut the amendment which the Minister of Justice is willing to accept does not require the Grand Trunk to incur the liability entailed by subscribing for the stock, and it carefully eliminates the words ' payable in cash at par.' It is, therefore, carefully designed to permit the Grand Trunk Company to acquire $24,900,000 of stock for any normal consideration that the two companies, different in name, though in reality the same, may agree upon between themselves. I am unable to accept the amendment which the government suggests, because it so emasculates my amendment that it takes from it everything of value, and enables the Grand Trunk to obtain the complete control of this railway, without putting more than a few dollars into it. If that is the policy of the government, let us understand It. The policy of the government, as suggested by the alteration handed to me by the Minister of Justice, is, that no matter what comes of this contract, the Grand Trunk Company must have liberty to acquire nearly $25,000,000 of this stock at any consideration that may be arranged between these two companies, which, according to the statement made from the treasury benches over and over again, though different in name, are the same in reality. And after all, the company which is obtaining the benefit of this contract with the government is the Grand Trunk Company of Canada. So far as I could gather from the attitude of the government to-day and yesterday, it intends to establish a so-called National Transcontinental Railway, and to place the line absolutely under the control of a railway which has its chief terminal and its only winter terminal, not in the Dominion of Canada, but in the United States of America. That is the first part of the policy of |
the government, and the second part of their policy is to deliberately permit the Grand Trunk Railway Company to divert to any extent which they desire Canadian traffic from Canadian routes and from Canadian ports. That is perfectly plain, because I got no answer from the treasury benches when I repeatedly asked, what reason there was for not imposing upon the .Grand Trunk Railway Company the same restrictions as to the diversion of traffic which are imposed upon jthe Grand Trunk Pacific Company. I challenge the ministry to give any answer now. I ask my right hon. friend to give one single reason which is not applicable to the Grand Trunk Railway Company with greater force in that regard than it is applicable to the Grand Trunk Pacific. I pointed out yesterday that the danger of diversion of traffic was not through the Grand Trunk Pacific, but through the Grand Trunk at North Bay, at Gravenhurst, at Winnipeg, and even at Quebec and Montreal. The Minister of Trade and Commerce recognized this danger, but the only answer I got was from the Minister of Finance who was put up to talk about dispute under contracts of fifteen or twenty years ago, and from the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) who was put up to talk about grades. Another feature of the policy of the government seems to be to deliberately frame the present Bill and contract so that the Grand Trunk may he enabled to construct a line in the great North-west of Canada at no cost to itself, except the guaranteeing of bonds representing one-fourth the cost of construction. The Grand Trunk obtains the absolute control of that road in the North-west ; it guarantees the issue of bonds to the extent of one-quarter the cost, but it enters into no other covenant or stipulation with the government in return for that great privilege. The fourth feature of the government's policy is to create $25,000,000 of common stock in order that $24,900,000, of that stock may be obtained by the Grand Trunk Railway for a mere nominal consideration to be arranged between the two companies which, according to the declaration of more than one member of the government, are, after all, in effect, only one company. That is what the gentlemen on the treasury benches call making the Grand Trunk Railway Company . * In ' and ' of ' this contract. Well, it is ' in ' and ' of ' this contract in a very peculiar sense. It makes no stipulation with the government; it is at liberty to divert traffic as it sees fit ; it is at liberty to use its own terminals at Portland, and it is at liberty to acquire the controlling interest in the Grand Trunk Pacific for a mere nominal consideration. In return for all that, the Grand Trunk guarantees the issue of bonds to the extent of one-fourth of the cost. We have been told that, from the standpoint of the country's interest, this

is one of the most magnificent and praiseworthy enterprises that any government ever entered into. At an early stage of this debate, the Minister of the Interior pointed out that as regards the western division of this railway there is absolutely no possibility of failure. He spoke of the 50,000,000 acres that are to be opened for settlement in the North-west; he spoke of hundreds of thousands of immigrants pouring into that country ; he declared that the conditions which faced the Canadian Pacific Railway when they built theii road on the prairies were far more unfavourable than those which to-day confront the Grand Trunk Pacific. He demonstrated conclusively that the building of this railway through that western country was one of the best business propositions that had ever been undertaken by anj company. The Grand Trunk is to have-placed at its disposal that splendid business proposition ; it is to have a road built through the North-west at no cost or risk to itself, except the guaranteeing of the bonds for one-quarter of the cost, and in return for that, what does the Grand Trunk give ? It gives no stipulation to the government that it will not divert traffic to American channels. Is the government willing to impose upon it any restriction or condition in that regard ? The government is not willing. It is to acquire a controlling interest in the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. Is the government ready to say that that interest must be purchased for a substantial consideration ? The government is not willing, because we are now dealing with an amendment which seeks to impose on the Grand Trunk Railway Company an obligation to subscribe for that stock at par. The government say they are willing to accept the amendment in this emasculated form, by which it will still be left open to these two companies, in reality one company, to arrange the terms between themselves by which that stock shall be acquired by the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Under these circumstances, in view of this attitude of the government, I am not prepared to accept for one moment this amendment in the form in which it has been handed to me by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, and I propose to take the sense of the committee on the amendment in the form in which I first submitted it.	[DOT]

I beg leave to move that the following be substituted for the amendment
2. Notwithstanding anything in this Act or in the said agreement contained, His Majesty the King a-ctimg in res-pect of -the government of Canada shall not be bound or obliged to perform, carry out or fulfl-l any of the covenants, undertakings, conditions or stipulations in the said agreement contained on behalf of His Majesty the King acting as aforesaid unless and until -the Grand Trunk Railway Company of

Canada sha-ll -have entered into an agreement with His Majesty -the King acting as aforesaid by which the said Grand Trunk Railway Company shall covenant and agree to acquire and take the -common stock of -the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to the amount of not less than $24,900,000 as in clause 27 -of said agreement provided.
3. T.he Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall hold ith-e -said common stock -to the amount aforesaid so acquired and taken as aforesaid during the entire -term of the lease mentioned in -clause 20 of the said agreement, and -so long as any of the bonds guaranteed by the government under the terms of the said agreement shall remain outstanding and unpaid, and no pledge, transfer or conveyance of any part of -the said stock -during the said period shall be valid or effectual.
My bon. friend, in moving bis amendment, said yesterday in the course of the debate that no answer bad been made to the contention of the opposition that the policy of the government was to allow the diversion of traffic to American ports. I hope my bon. friend will not suppose that if we did not answer bis argument more fully, it was because we did not regard it as serious ; but we recognized that all these matters bad been fully and repeatedly discussed before we went into committee on the Bill. We do not consider that the policy of the government is calculated to in any way allow the diversion of traffic to American ports to go on; but this Bill was framed and this contract entered into for the express purpose of preventing that diversion which has been going on heretofore under the railway policy adopted in past years. We think the effect of this Bill will be to prevent that diversion from Port Arthur to Buffalo and New York, and from Montreal to Portland and Boston ; and we submit that the policy of the opposition, as proposed by the leader in bis scheme, would have had the effect of confirming that diversion, which would necessarily have taken place. The original Grand Trunk scheme would have had the same effect, and of this scheme the opposition approved. The scheme of the government on the contrary, is to have a line of railway extending from Winnipeg to Quebec and from Quebec to Moncton, which will have the effect, if geographical conditions count for anything, of carrying the trade to the ports of the maritime provinces. Nothing that we can say in answer to the contention of the hon. leader of the opposition can be stronger than the terms of the contract itself. By the terms of this contract the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company are to construct this road from Winnipeg to the Pacific ocean ; and in order to prevent the Grand Trunk Railway Company, as a result of its control over the Grand Trunk Pacific, diverting the trade to American ports, the government are to own the road from Winnipeg eastward, and to fix the conditions under which it shall be operated. The condition under which this aid is given to the Grand Trunk Pacific

Company is that it shall carry its trade through Canadian channels to Quebec and Moncton. That is provided in the agreement, and the company entered into this agreement and accepted aid on this condition. Any government in this country that would fail to see that the spirit and the letter of that contract are complied with would fail in the performance of its duty to the people of Canada. The Grand Trunk Pacific Company concur in the preamble of this contract, which states that the very object of this measure is to have a Canadian road on Canadian territory to develop trade through Canadian ports. Then, you have that clause in the agreement which says that the condition on which we grant this assistance is that the company shall carry the freight to Canadian ports. Surely the government of Canada is strong enough to see that these conditions shall be carried out. So long as this government is in power, these conditions shall be carried out ; and if hon. gentlemen opposite should come into power, the duty and responsibility would rest upon them, and we have a right to assume, in view of all their contentions in this debate, that they will see that they are carried out. The hon. gentleman says that the Grand Trunk Company is going to construct the railway in the North-west from Winnipeg to the Pacific for its own benefit and at no expense to itself. It seems to me that we have rehearsed the terms of this contract often enough to understand what the true conditions are.

My hon. friend is not stating it quite correctly. I said that the road to be built in the North-west would be absolutely controlled by the Grand Trunk Company, which would incur no obligation for its construction, except the guarantee of one-fourth of the bonds.

I accept that statement. What are the conditions for the construction of the road from Winnipeg to the Pacific coast ? The conditions are that the road shall be built by the Grand Trunk Pacific, that to aid in the construction of that road the government of Canada agree to guarantee a first issue of bonds to the extent of 75 per cent of the cost of construction, provided the cost of construction ishall not exceed in the prairie section $13,000 and in the mountain section $30,000 a mile, and that the Grand Trunk Railway Company, not for its benefit, but for the greater security of the government, shall guarantee all the second issue of bonds to an amount sufficient to complete the construction of the road. That provision, it seems to me, was intended or designed to, and in effect will, protect the government in this first issue of bonds. The guarantee of the government in so far as this first issue of bonds is concerned is in this position, that if default is made with respect to any of the obligations on which
i
this first guarantee is given the effect will be necessarily that the road will pass into the hands of the government. That is we become owners of that road to the construction of which we have contributed seventy-five per cent of the cost. And what is the result of the second issue of bonds ? The second issue of bonds then will be absolutely of no value in the hands of the holders, whoever they may be, except in so far as the Grand Trunk Railway Company may make them of some value. Therefore the result is that the Grand Trunk Railway must make that road a success, must see to the performance of all' the conditions under the contract, because, otherwise, they will be responsible for the entire value of that second issue of bonds. In addition to that our first issue of bonds is guaranteed by a mortgage, not only upon the road-which for the sake of argument vve will assume will cost $100,000,000-not only upon the $75,000,000 contributed by the government, but upon the entire $100,000,000 which the road will cost for construction and also upon the $20,000,000 of equipment supplied by the Grand Trunk Pacific. Thus we will contribute $75,000,000, and in case of default the whole road and equipment of a total value of $120,000,000, will fall into our hands ; that is the contract and that is not disputed. I ask is it in the interests of the government or of the Grand Trunk Railway that this provision is made ? Is it in the interest of the government that we should have the Grand Trunk Railway as guarantor of the second issue of bonds, and that the Grand Trunk Railway should be placed in the position that, in the event of default of the first issue, the whole second issue should go by the board ; we take the road with the total equipment, the Grand Trunk Railway take the obligation to pay the second issue of bonds.
With respect to the extension of the road from Winnipeg eastward, the road is to be built by the government, and when it is completed the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company will lease it for the period mentioned in the agreement. If the road had been built, owned and operated by the Grand Trunk Pacific, that company being under the control of the Grand Trunk Company, as hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House assume, what would have happened ? That road would have been built by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company only so far as it suited their purpose and as would enable them to divert their trade to North Bay and to Montreal and Portland. What is going on now would have continued and hon. gentlemen opposite wanted that to go on ; they asked for it, and approved of that policy. We on the other hand, say to them: We shall construct a road from Winnipeg to Quebec and from Quebec to Moncton, and will make it a condition of granting aid towards the construction of the western end

that the eastern end is operated. They have to operate it and in default of operating it they forfeit $5,000,000 worth of equipment. And if they are obliged to operate that road are they not obliged to see that it pays. They have not only to pay the cost of maintenance and operation of the road, but also three per cent on the cost of construction. If the Grand Trunk Pacific is in reality another name for the Grand Trunk, as hon. gentlemen oppoisite state, are the Grand Trunk Company not under an obligation to see that that road is operated in such a way that they may derive a revenue sufficient to maintain and operate it and also to pay the three per cent interest ? If they are to do all these things they must get traffic for the road. If they are going to divert the traffic to Portland and United States ports what are they to do with the eastern end of their line ? Where are they to get the traffic which will- enable them to fulfil all the obligations under the agreement ? It seems to me-and I do not say this with any desire to be discourteous to my hon. friends -that we have gone over this ground so frequently that nothing can now be said that will not be idle reiteration. I take it that we must stand by this agreement. Hon, gentlemen opposite put one construction on the agreement, and I wish to say, speaking not in a parliamentary sense, that I believe my hon. friends would not speak as they do if they did not believe in the correctness of the interpretation they put upon the contract. They conceive the agreement to mean what they say it means, and we interpret it to mean what we say ; the country must decide between us. We must stand by this agreement and abide by it.
If we must stand by the agreement which the government has made, why does the Minister of Justice himself propose amending it ?

I propose to amend it myself, with respect to two provisions of the agreement, and I will give my reasons for doing so. One clause provides that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company shall secure from the Grand Trunk Railway Company the guarantee of the second issue of the bonds; another clause provides that the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall acquire the common stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to the extent of $25,000,000. Hon. gentlemen opposite say that the Grand Trunk Railway Company not being parties to the agreement, are not bound by these two stipulations, and on the qther hand, we argue that while these two provisions are not binding on the Grand Trunk Company, as tbe contract stands in law, in effect they are binding upon them because these two conditions are conditions precedent to our obligation to guarantee the bonds. That is to say that unless the Grand Trunk Railway

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Company take the $25,000,000 of common stock and guarantee the second issue of bonds we are not obliged to do anything under the agreement. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition says that this does not result from the wording of the agreement. He says that it should be made clear. Now I have some regard for the leader of the opposition-I speak with all deference, using these words in his presence-I have some regard for him, and when he expresses doubt as to a contract, I want to set that doubt at rest. He has expressed a doubt as to this contract, and I want to eliminate that doubt and to make it absolutely clear, as we intended it should be, that the Grand Trunk Railway Company should do two things, first, take stock to the extent of $25,000,000, and second, undertake to guarantee the second issue of bonds. That is our intention; that was the intention of the parties to the agreement; I want to make that clear and that is the object of my amendment. I do not consider that by accepting such an amendment I am doing anything that is not praiseworthy. On the contrary, I think it is a complete answer to my hon. friends who say that we bring an iron-clad agreement to this House and will not accept any amendment. We bring the contract here to get such assistance in perfecting it as we can get; the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) say that there is room for doubt on this point, and we want to set that doubt at rest. That is the object in accepting the amendment.
Why not accept the exact provisions of the amendment ?
We do not agree as to the length we should go.

My hon. friend the Minister of Justice will acquit me from any desire to be guilty of tiresome reiteration and if I do reiterate sometimes in this discussion it is because I doubt if I make myself clear to hon. gentlemen opposite, for when they rise to answer statements I have made they usually answer something which I never said at all, and I will take one or two minutes for the purpose of making my meaning clear. I pointed out that when the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway brings freight in the winter from the Northwest to Quebec or to Montreal it can carry that freight 297 miles from Montreal to Portland or 318 miles from Quebec to Portland, and it will be carrying that freight over its own lines and will be earning the entire tolls that will be charged for that distance. In lieu of that you will have the project of carrying that freight to the city of St. John or the city of Halifax in the maritime provinces. If you accept the extreme limit that has been put forward by tile Minister of Finance as to the saving of distance by the new line, you have a dis-

tauce of between 460 miles and 489 miles from Quebec to the city of St. John, and a distance of 586 miles from Quebec to the city of Halifax. Now, will it not be more in the interest of the Grand Trunk Railway that that freight shall be carried over its own line for that short distance to Portland than that it shall be carried partly over the lines of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway and partly over the line of the Intercolonial Railway to Halifax or St. John ? That is a plain question for the consideration of any business man in this House. Where do the interests of the Grand Trunk Railway in that regard lie ? Will any hon. gentleman on the other side of the House venture so far as to rise in his place and say that it will not be in the interests of the Grand Trunk Railway Company that that freight shall go to Portland ?
What is the distance between Quebec and Portland by way of the Grand Trunk Railway ?
The distance, as I understand it by way of the Grand Trunk Railway, is 318 miles.
From Quebec ?
From Quebec. Does the right hon. gentleman controvert that ?
Yes, I do.
What is the distance ?
The distance between Portland and Montreal is 300 miles, and the distance between Quebec and Richmond is 100 miles, so that the distance between Quebec and Portland must be about 400 miles.

I am not talking about the distance between Quebec and Richmond. I am talking about the distance between Montreal and Portland. It is given by the Grand Trunk Railway in their timetable as 297 miles. The distance from Quebec to Portland via Richmond, as stated in the Grand Trunk Railway time-table, is 318 miles. Is my right hon. friend in a position to controvert that ?

The distance between Montreal and Portland is 300 miles. The distance between Quebec and Richmond where the road joins with the road from Montreal to Portland is 100 miles, so that there is a distance between Quebec and Portland of 400 miles.

May I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) how he would expect grain to get to Montreal and to be diverted to Portland because the distance from the point at which the railway would intersect the transcontinental line north of 375
North Bay to Montreal is much longer than it would be from that point to Quebec ?

I do not know whether it will go that way or not, but I know it has been alleged in this House by members of the government and by hon. gentlemen speaking on the other side of the House that there will be a branch built from this eastern division connecting with the city of Montreal and I understood that it was expected that a very considerable amount of freight would come from the west and go east by way of Montreal.
From the poiut where the road will be deflected to Montreal will such distance to Montreal be greater than it will be to Quebec ?

I really do not know because no one up to the present time has been able to give any idea as to the location of this line or as to the distance from any point on the eastern division to Montreal and therefore my hon. friend (Mr. Heyd) knows when he asks that question that it is impossible to answer it. Whether you take it from Montreal or Quebec you are exactly in the same position, because, if 1 am right about the distance from Quebec to Portland, it is only twenty-one miles greater than the distance from Montreal to Portland. Assuming that I am right, and I would be very glad to be corrected if I am not, you have Quebec 318 miles distant from Portland and Montreal 297 miles distant from Portland, while Quebec is distant from Halifax, assuming that all the saving the government expects is realized, 586 miles. 1 make that up this way : 400 miles from Quebec to Moncton, taking the estimate of the hon. Minister of Finance, and 186 miles from Moncton to Halifax, making a total of 586 miles. From Quebec to Moncton it is 400 miles and from Moncton to St. John 89 miles. You may make a saving of twenty miles by running the line from Chipman to St. John, but allowing for that, you have a distance from Quebec to St. John of from 460 to 470 miles. I was going on to ask when I was interrupted :	Will or will it not pay the
Grand Trunk Railway Company to carry that freight over its own line to Portland and earn the whole of the tolls upon it or will the company be more likely to send the freight by way of Moncton and thence over the Intercolonial Railway to Halifax. My hon. friend states that the tolls are the same. The very fact that the tolls are the same will make it all the more in the interest of the Grand Trunk Railway Company to take it to Portland, because, even assuming that the Grand Trunk Railway Company has an interest of a substantial character in the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company you will have freight carried for the same tolls 489 miles to St. John, or 586 miles to Halifax, w-hen it can be carried by the Grand



Trunk Railway Company over its own line 318 miles from Quebec to Portland or 297 miles from Montreal to Portland. It seems to me perfectly obvious that there is very great danger as far as the Grand Trunk Railway is concerned that it will use all possible efforts to divert this traffic from St. John and Halifax to Portland as it has done in the past. I have repeatedly said that I do not blame the Grand Trunk Railway for looking after its own interests. It has great terminals at Portland and it wants to earn all the money possible for its shareholders, but it Is the duty of this government to see that the Grand Trunk Railway Company receiving in effect this aid for the building of this road shall not divert the traffic from Canadian channels. That is only one point of danger that I have pointed out. I have mentioned another point and it is the danger on the shore of the Georgian bay where the Grand Trunk Railway will take the traffic and carry it to Portland without let or hindrance. I have pointed out the danger at North Bay and Gravenhurst. I have pointed out the danger mentioned by the right hon Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) of the connection between Chicago and Winnipeg and the acquisition of freight by the Grand Trunk Railway Company which has been gathered up by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company in the west to be diverted to American lines. I have pointed out all these dangers but the hon. Minister of Justice contents himself with using a general expression to the effect that sufficient guarantees and stipulations have been inserted in this contract. No guarantee or stipulation as far as the Grand Trunk Railway is concerned has been inserted in the contract. Therefore,-although these dangers exist, they have not been provided for at all. The hon. Minister of Justice seemed to think that I was arguing in some way or other that it was not in the interests of the country that the guarantee of bonds by the Grand Trunk Company should be executed. I am not arguing anything of the kind. My hon. friend also touches upon the security for the operation of the eastern division. Is there anything in that provision in regard to the eastern division that prevents the Grand Trunk Railway from doing what I have just stated it would be its interest to do ? I see nothing in this contract in regard to the operation of this eastern division which touches that question at all. Therefore. it does not seem that the remarks of my hon. friend in regard to that feature of the contract had any relevancy. I do not want to go into that as it does not seem relevant to the question, but does the hon. gentleman think that $5,000,000 worth of rolling stock is a sufficient guarantee for the operation of the road and the payment of rental ? In fifty years it might amount to $100,000,000.
We have recourse under the agreement.
You can only take over the eastern division.
No, we can take over the whole road. The Grand Trunk Railway owns the whole thing.
If this is subject to $100,000,000 of a mortgage your security would be more imaginary than real. The government would have guaranteed the bonds to the extent of 75 per cent.

I think we would be very glad to take over the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Mr. BORDEN) (Halifax). I do not know about, that. Perhaps so, but we are talking about, security. The only security there would be would be the value over and above the $100,000,000. We do not know what the value of the security might be.

In answer to the right hon. gentleman (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laur-ier) I can give the exact distances from Quebec and Montreal to Portland. Prom Portland to Richmond, which is common to the two lines, it is 220 miles ; from Richmond to Montreal, it is 77 miles, or through from Portland to Montreal 297 miles. Prom Richmond to Quebec is 971 miles, making from Portland to Quebec 317i miles, just twenty and a half miles difference.
I over-stated it, then, about half a mile.

I understood the Minister of Justice just now to say that the government, in case of default by the Grand Trunk Pacific of the rental and other obligations that were incurred for operating the eastern division, will take over the western division, subject to the amount of bonds guaranteed by the government.
We can take it over, but if they fail to perform their obligations, all the assets of the Grand Trunk Pacific will be liable for the indebtedness, subject to the mortgages.

This contract has been altered, evidently, since I was here on Friday, because the government permits the Grand Trunk to issue bonds to the extent of 25 per cent, which become a second charge, with the consent of the government, on the whole western division. Now, the Minister of Justice says that the government have the security of the western division for the operation of the eastern division.
I did uot say anything of the sort.

I think the minister will find that is what he stated, but I am quite

sure lie did not mean that. He said, subject to the guarantee of the bonds. I want to make that very clear, that-the government has not that security, subject to the government guarantee of the bonds.
I understood the Minister of Justice to say, and I accepted his statement, that there was security on the western division for the operation of the road.

There is security to this extent, that if they fail in the operation of the eastern end, of course they would become liable under the contract for the rental, in which case we would have the liability of the Grand Trunk Pacific, for which liability of course all their assets would be available, and part of their assets would be the western extension. That is what I said.

I thought my hon. friend distinctly said that there was some charge on the western division, but there is not any charge. Of course, my hon. friend recognizes that all it amounts to is that there is a covenant, and we can enforce that covenant against any property of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway that we can find.
That is it, outside liabilities.

I understood the Minister of Justice to say that if the Grand Trunk Pacific refused to operate the eastern section they would forfeit their equipment-I presume that is the equipment of the eastern section to the value of $5,000,000. Now, the only security which the government have, as I understand, is a second mortgage on that equipment-am I right in that ?

To this extent, that the first mortgage on the equipment is ours, so we have the first and second mortgage. We have the first mortgage on all the equipment of the road to SGCuie us against loss, and. our guarantee of the bonds for the construction of the western end; and then, in addition to that, we have a second mortgage for the equipment of the eastern end with respect to the operation of the road.
If the Grand Trunk Pacific lefused to operate the eastern section, how could the government realize on 'hat second mortgage ? How would they proceed to realize on it ?
They would proceed to realize upon the second mortgage by simply foreclosing, a very simple proceeding.
They would have to deal with the first mortgage first, before they could foreclose.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The Minister of Justice moves an amendment to the amendment, as follows :
2.	Notwithstanding anything in this Act or in the said agreement contained, His Majesty the King, acting in respect of the government of Canada shall not be bound or obliged to perform, carry out or fulfil any of the covenants, undertakings, conditions or stipulations in the said agreement contained on behalf of His Majesty the King acting as aforesaid, unless and until the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada -shall have entered into an agreement with His Majesty the King acting as aforesaid by which the said Grand Trunk Railway Company shall covenant and agree to acquire and take the -common stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to the amount of not less than $24,900,000, as in clause 27 of said agreement provided.
3.	The Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall hold the -said common -stock to the amount aforesaid and so acquired and taken as aforesaid during the entire -term of the lease mentioned in clau-se 20 of the said agreement, and so long as any of the bo-n-ds guaranteed by the government under the terms of the said agreement shall remain outstanding and unpaid, and no -p-ledge, transfer or conveyance of any part of the said stock during said period shall be valid or effectual.

I waited to bear the reply of the Minister of Justice to the statement made by the leader of the opposition, namely, that we are, after all, making a contract with the Grand Trunk Railway. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company is a mere cipher, and a mere coloufable matter in the whole thing. It is admitted that the Grand Trunk Railway Company is, after all, the moving power'of tb-e whole affair from start to finish. The Grand Trunk Railway Company acquires complete control of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. Therefore, any contract that is made with the Grand Trunk Pacific will have no effect, because that company is under the control of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Now, it has been pointed out by the Leader of the opposition that it is to the interest of the Grand Trunk Railway Company to carry freight over their own lines. It has -been pointed out that if even grain or any other freight were brought to the city of Montreal or the city of Quebec, it is in the interest of the Grand Trunk Railway Company to bring it to Portland, because the difference in the distance between Quebec and Portland and between Montreal and Portland is a mere fraction. The Minister of Justice laid great stress upon the fact that the freight would be carried to Quebec and then it would go to St John or Halifax. But it is pointed out that there is -absolutely no difference in the mileage, or that the difference is infinites-mally small, whether you go from Quebec to Portland or from Montreal to Portland. If you had taken it to the city of Quebec, and could show that you had placed it then nearer Halifax or St. John than to Portland, there might he some strong reasons urged

that you had taken it beyond that point where it could possibly go through other than Canadian channels. But when you reach Quebec by way of this transcontinental railway, you are as close to Portland as when you reach Montreal over the old Grand Trunk line. The Grand Trunk Railway Company will, of course, take the freight over its own line. It would be madness for a man to suppose that the Grand Trunk Railway Company, in becoming guarantors-they are more than guarantors, they have the control of the stock, they will control the whole operation of the road, and they will make ever}' part of the Grand Trunk Pacific feeders for the lines in tie, east which belong to the Grand Trunk Railway Company proper.		 , .
No person could find fault with that, but what we do find fault with, is that this is a bad bargain. Even if the traffic were carried over the Grand Trunk Pacific from Winnipeg to Quebec, it is in as much danger of going to Portland as if it were carried to Montreal. The distance from Quebec to Portland, as compared with the distance from Montreal to Portland is so small, as to make it certain that when you have that freight at Quebec, you have not carried it past the danger point. And in this consideration, 1 am leaving out of the question the fact, that distance from Quebec to St. John or Halifax is infinitely greater than it is to Portland. Every one knows that it is in the interests of the Grand Trunk, when they have this traffic at Quebec to take it along the line of least resistance, and every one knows that it is to their interests to take it to Portland. Whether this traffic is carried over the railway from Winnipeg to Quebec, or whether it is carried via North Bay. it is not unreasonable to ask that in either case, the Grand Trunk Railway, which derives the real benefit under this contract, should be bound to take it through Canadian ports. The amendment proposed by the leader of the opposition is the only safeguard the people of Canada can have, that Canadian traffic shall go through Canadian channels to Canadian ports. Outside of our political leanings, which no doubt have great influence upon us here, the question seems to me so plain, that it is not arguable from the other point of view.

The government exhibit an extraordinary spectacle to the country in connection with this matter. They present a Bill for the ratification of parliament, and they tell us that no amendment can be made to it because it is a binding contract signed by both parties. However, when a proposal to amend it is made by the leader of the opposition, the Minister of Justice, says, that in deference to the high legal ability of my hon. friend (Mr. Borden) he is proposed to accept that amendment. But when it comes to accepting the amendment, lie
Mr, CLANCY.
accepts it by moving an amendment of his own which is quite different from the amendment itself. If the Minister of Justice entertains a high respect for the legal acumen of the leader of the opposition, why does he not leave the amendment in the legal phraseology presented by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden) ? If the Minister of Justice did that, we would have much more confidence that it would accomplish the end which the leader of the opposition desires. I direct attention to the extraordinary spectacle of the government amending their own contract, after they have signed and sealed it, thereby implying that their contract, which they have many times declared binds the Grand Trunk to carry out all its obligations, is, after all, not perfect or complete, and that the leader of the opposition has to step in to render it a better contract. That in itself is sufficient to discredit the whole contract. Would the Prime Minister, or the Minister of Justice, tell me, what object the government had in view in compelling the Grand Trunk to secure this $25,000,000 of common stock ?
To practically force them to take an interest in this road, and to have their interests bound with it.

If the interest be of any real value it ought to be worth $25,000,000. If they acquire this $25,000,000 worth of common stock for the use of a few terminals, that only represents a value of a few thousand dollars to them, of what use is their interest in the Grand Trunk Pacific ? If they have to pay 100 cents on the dollar for that stock, they will have an interest of $25,000,000 in the new enterprise, but if they can get that stock for a few thousand dollars, their interest amounts to nothing. The Minister of Justice tells us that they will be compelled to acquire that stock.
There is a great difference between acquiring stock and subscribing for stock and paying a hundred cents in the dollar for it. If you compel me to pay Into a bank to the* credit of a company $1,000,000, that represents $1,000,000 to me; but if you allow me the privilege of playing cards for that $1,000,000, and I am fortunate enough to get it by the game and for which it cost me nothing, it does not represent anything of value to me, and I would not be istanding in the same relation to the company. If I got $1,000,000 of stock for something that represented very little value to me, I could not be regarded as having the same substantial interest in the road that I would have if I paid cash for that stock. I wish to ask another question in reference to this whole contract; that is, why do we have all this confusion ? Why is this agreement complicated by mixing up the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and the Government Transcontinental Railway ? Why not throw

out the Grand Trunk Pacific Company and deal with the Grand Trunk Railway Company 1 This confusion and mixing up of these three railways makes the whole contract very difficult to understand. Why all this confusion ? There must he some object that is not plain to the ordinary mind. I fear that that object is to enable the Grand Trunk Company to accomplish in an indirect way what they could not accomplish in a plain and direct way. I think that is unfair to the members of this House and to the people of this country. What is the government's object ? Why do they not place a Bill before this House so plain that every member, whether a lawyer or a layman, and whether possessed of great acumen and intelligence or very little of it, could understand it, and so that he would know what he is doing, and his constituents would know ? Why do we have the Bill in this obscure and ambiguous language so that even a Philadelphia lawyer would be unable to understand what the outcome will be if we give legal sanction to it ? We have the government to-day dishonouring their own contract. Although they have argued day after day that there was not a weak feature in the contract, that it was perfect from beginning to end, yet now at the last moment, we have the Minister of Justice proposing an amendment to the amendment of the leader of the opposition, thereby discrediting the whole scheme. I think that is not very creditable to the government, and is not likely to inspire confidence in this House or in the country that they correctly understood the contract wheu they made it, or that if legal effect is given to it, it will accomplish what they have claimed for it.

I feel anxious about this contract as a maritime province man. The people of the maritime provinces have for thirty-six years been waiting for the fulfilment of the promises of confederation. Now, we want them fulfilled, and the hon. leader of the opposition has asked why should we give the Grand Trunk Railway Company the privileges of a principal and hot require from them all the obligations of a principal. That is the question to which we want an answer. The Minister of Justice appears pained that we are endeavouring to understand this question. I am bound as a maritime province man to understand it thoroughly, because when the government of this country undertakes to make this enormous expenditure of money, if this expenditure fails, we in the maritime provinces can never expect for twenty or forty years again to be in a position to demand from the people of Canada the fulfilment of the terms of confederation. Therefore, as a maritime province man, I am interested in finding out why the Grand Trunk Railway Company is not a principal in this matter. The Prime Minister, in opening this
debate, said: We have the Grand Trunk Railway Company behind us. If that is so,
1 want to ask him or the Minister of Justice why do you not make the Grand Trunk Railway Company the principal in this matter instead of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company ? The Minister of Justice knows that this objection is not raised simply by the political opponents in this parliament. The other day the hon. Minister of Finance received from the merchants of Halifax, irrespective of politics a telegram Risking him what was the meaning of clause 42, by which it was permitted to gentlemen who wanted to use this railway the right to route their traffic otherwise than over this railway ? That telegram was signed by Liberals as well as Conservatives, so that the government must realize that this objection is not a political objection. Therefore they must not be surprised if we press this question. The hon. Minister of Justice thinks he understands this contract ; but I am one of those who understand a contract better every hour that it is discussed. The question we in the maritime provinces want answered is why the Grand Trunk Railway Company is not put in this contract as principal ? The business men of the whole country want an answer to that question, and it is a question which I think the government should answer. The government should be frank with parliament and give its reasons. If the government will justify to me why the Grand Trunk Railway should stand aside and a dummy toe put forward in the person of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, I am fair enough to admit that they acted wisely. But the government must face the question, and explain to the maritime provinces why they contract with a dummy instead of the principal. Some people say that the Grand Trunk Railway did not want to assume the responsibility of operating the eastern section, but only wanted to control the western section, and that therefore it refused to be a party to this contract. It is pretended that the object of the Grand Trank Railway is to drop the eastern section and not operate it and let the government look to the Grand Trank Pacific Railway to make good the default. It is for the government to dissipate this suspicion by proving that no such contingency need be anticipated. The time is ripe for the building of a new transcontinental line, but it must be a line that will meet the present requirements of our national life. If you undertake to launch Canada into the building of a new transcontinental line which will not meet those *requirements, you will throw back the national development of Canada some twenty-five or fifty years. No doubt Canada, with her giant strength, will be able to recover from any false step, but what is the use of committing errors and crippling the country ? I appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite.

Surely they do no want any mistakes made. The government after all are only some fifteen men in the cabinet, and it is not possible that in these negotiations they could have foreseen every difficulty. They should therefore, not hold up this contract as something perfect and sacred which nobody must touch, but should be prepared to admit any imperfection that the right of discussion may reveal. My hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, has pointed out difficulties. Let us remove them in order that there may be no possibility of mistake. I am convinced that if the government had left the Grand Trunk Railway out of the scheme entirely, if the government had contracted with an absolutely new company, and compelled it to build from the Atlantic to the Pacific, there would be no danger of the freight going over that railway being diverted to an American port. That company would be interested in taking every pound of freight down to the port of Halifax. No question of routing to Portland could possibly arise, and there would have been no necessity for any high-sounding clause about the company receiving its aid upon high national grounds and being bound to carry its freight to Halifax, because the company would not be in a position to do otherwise. But this hybrid system makes the introduction of this routing clause necessary. It does not follow, however, that the clause will be effective. We know by experience that railway companies will not do anything no matter what may be the agreement, which is not in their own interests. They will always contrive to find some means to evade any such agreement. That much-vaunted clause requiring freight charges to be the same to Halifax as to Portland, I regard as the most disastrous clause in the whole agreement. From Montreal to Halifax is 850 miles, and from Montreal to Portland is 297 miles. If the Grand Trunk Railway is required to haul freight from Montreal to Halifax, that will mean 553 miles more of a haul than to Portland. The Grand Trunk Railway will therefore take every means possible to avoid carrying out that obligation. Every one of its customers, if he wants to stand well with the company, will route his freight to Portland rather than compel the company to haul it 553 miles further at the same price. We therefore, in the maritime provinces regard that clause as a direct blow at our interest. Suppose the freight passes Montreal and goes to Quebec, from Quebec to Halifax is 586 miles and from Quebec to Portland is 318 miles, so that the Grand Trunk Railway will have a longer haul of 168 miles to Halifax than to Portland. Gan any one doubt that every pressure possible will be exercised by the company to get its clients to route to Portland ? Consequently, in that routing clause there is nothing but danger to the maritime provinces. This agreement may perhaps bo advantageous to Quebec, but I would ask Mr. IJOURLT5Y.
the right hon. the Prime Minister and the hon. the Minister of Justice not to be sectional and to remember that there are other interests besides those of Quebec. The interests of the maritime provinces are vastly superior. No country was ever worth anything which had not great maritime interests, and if you were to cut off the maritime provinces and we were to declare our independence, the provinces of Ontario and Quebec would become back yards to the maritime provinces and nothing more. I do not care to make these assertions, because I have always stood here against anything sectional. I am a Quebec man as much as a Nova Scotia man, and a British Columbia man as much as an Ontario man. But if we are driven to make sectional issues, I am bound to say that the maritime provinces to-day control the destinies of Canada. No nation has ever been worth anything in the history of the world which is not a maritime nation. Your people must come down to the sea.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would call the attention of the hon. gentleman to the fact that he is going outside the point at issue.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that what I am saying is germane to the subject.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must call the hon. gentleman to order. He is wandering away from the question under discussion.

I am always ready to bow to your decision, Air. Chairman. The question before us now is whether a sufficient security has been taken or sufficient provision made to compel this railway to carry freight to our ocean ports. The basis of this proposition was laid by the hon. the First Alinister when he said that , this was to be a Canadian line from ocean to ocean. What we are seeking is to compel the Grand Trunk Railway to pay for this stock and thus have a vital interest in carrying the freight from the west to the ocean port of Halifax. The Prime Minister and the Alinister of Justice must not think that because they live in the province of Quebec and have safeguarded the interests of the port of Quebec, they have also safeguarded the interests of the maritime- provinces. It appears to me as if this scheme had been engineered entirely in the interests of Quebec. The more I look at it the more I am convinced that it was engineered in the interests of Quebec and that not the slightest heed was paid to the maritime provinces. Those who put through the contract seemed to think that a few high-sounding words about this being a national enterprise and that the freights should consequently go to Canadian ports would be a sufficient sop for the people down by the sea. But they will find out their mistake. The maritime provinces have been looking

forward to a new national transcontinental line; and if this scheme would give us such a line it would have my hearty support. If the government had brought down an agreement with an entirely new company and a Canadian company, if they had selected a Canadian ocean port either St. John or Halifax, and if they had chosen a route through Canada that would be the shortest to the ocean for the freight of the west, I would have supported such a scheme. But because X find this scheme defective at every stage, because there are conditions in it fatal to the object it is intended to accomplish because it will not bring the trade to a Canadian maritime port, I am bound to oppose it. Every business man in the maritime provinces is hostile to the scheme. Hon. gentleman opposite may smile but when they will have to face an aroused public sentiment in the maritime provinces, whose interests are being betrayed in this contract-whether betrayed unwittingly or with malice aforethought does not change the fact-they will not find any occasion for smiling. The aspirations of the people in the maritime provinces must be consulted. We had a little rebellion at one time threatened in the province of Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman must not proceed to discuss matters which have no bearing on the question before the House.
I think in the interests of the Prime Minister, that my being called to order was perfectly justified.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman, having been called to order, might not proceed to discuss my decision of the Chair.

I am congratulating you, Sir, on the justice of your ruling. I think that it wa s a very timely ruling to protect the Finance Minister from any reference to his appeals to Nova Scotia, in former days, against this confederation. We are charged, on this side, with making factious opposition, but surely the government do not want to spend 8200,000,000 and then fail in the very purpose which the Prime Minister says he has so much at heart. We know that the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway did not realize what it was expected to do for the maritime provinces. We know that Sir Charles Tupper and Sir John Macdonald did not, in some measure, fulfil the promises they had made to those provinces in connection with that great transcontinental line. Then, I would say : Let us not repeat that error. Surely, now, when we have this great scheme before us, we should adopt every safeguard in order that there may be no complaints from the maritime provinces against this government for having made the same mistake as it has been stated other governments have made. I, therefore, ask the government to accept
not only this amendment, but several others, in order to carry out this view. Why should the Grand Trunk control this undertaking and not be responsible for its obligations ? This is a question which has been asked in the maritime provinces. The people in those provinces take the view that the Grand Trunk Railway Company do not want to become responsible for anything in connection with the eastern division, because they hold property which might be forfeited if they were parties to this agreement. They wanted to be in the position to get all the advantages possible from this scheme, to use the Grand Trunk Pacific to pull the chestnuts out of the fire, and then, when the chestnuts are out, if they are nicely browned, they will eat them, but if they are burned, they will let the Grand Trunk Pacific have them. We want to know why the old Grand Trunk Railway Company are to have all the advantages arising from this contract, and not be responsible for what is done on the eastern section, and I think the government have made a very curious contract in introducing a third party into the agreement, and not making them responsible or compelling them to assume any of the risk.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
We have heard a good deal from the legal gentlemen on both sides of the House in reference to this contract and to the amendment now before the House. I have carefully examined the amendment proposed by the leader of the opposition and the amendment to that amendment proposed by the Minister of Justice, and I find that the difference between them resolve themselves down to the difference between two words. In the amendment of the leader of the oposition the word ' subscribe ' is used. The Minister of Justice puts in the word 'acquire.' Now, what is the difference between these two words ; what is their significance, looked at from a business point of view ? The Minister of Justice pays great respect to the legal ability of the leader of the opposition, and I think he is right in doing so, judging from the different amendments that have been made by that gentleman to legislation presented to this House during the last two or three sessions. The difference is this: the word in the amendment proposed by the leader of the opposition means that if the Grand Trunk Railway subscribe for this $25,000,000 of stock, they are legally responsible for the payment of that amount for the benefit of the people of this country, should there be any failure on the part of the Grand Trunk Pacific to carry out the undertaking. But the proposition of the Minister of Justice absolves the Grand Trunk Railway Company from any legal liability whatever ; they simply can acquire that stock by any arrangement they may make with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. It may be handed over to them for $100 or $1,000, or any sum agreed upon between

them. If the Grand Trunk subscribe as stockholders, they will be legally responsible to the people of this country for the $25,000,000. Half a dozen persons may join themselves together, form a limited liability company with a capital stock of $50,000 or $100,000. and start a manufacturing concern. They may pay in only 10 per cent of the amount of the stock for which they subscribe ; but they are legally liable for the remaining 90 per cent, if the business requires it. After they have been in business for a few years, they may find it would pay them better to wind up the company than to pay in the balance of the stock and lose that money also ; but if the company fails in business, the creditors can call on the stockholders to pay up the balance of the subscribed capital in order to discharge the indebtedness of the company. What is the case with a banking institution ? You subscribe for stock, and you are liable for double the amount of the stock for which you subscribe. Why should it not be the same in this case ? The Grand Trunk Railway Company would subscribe for the $25,000,000 stock in the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and would pay in 25 per cent, or 10 per cent, or whatever might be required by the Grand Trunk Pacific in order to carry on this work. But if the Grand Trunk Pacific should fail in carrying out the obligation imposed upon it, then the people of this country, through the government, could call on the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway to compel the Grand Trunk Railway Company to pay up the $25,000,000 in order to discharge the indebtedness of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, the 3 per cent on the cost of building the road. That is the security we would have, if you would put in the word proposed by the leader of the opposition. The people of this country would then have a legal claim on the Grand Trunk Railway Company. But if you put in the word used by the Minister of Justice, then this clause is as big a fraud as calling this railway a transcontinental railway, when it ends at Moncton, not near the ocean at all. It is not a transcontinental railway, because at Moncton it has to connect with the Intercolonial Jtailway. And I say that the word ' acquii-e ' is as big a fraud on the people of this country. This clause will bear out the words of Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson, president of the Grand Trunk Railway, who said in England that the stockholders of the Grand Trunk Railway are not responsible in any way for this enterprise. The clause of the Minister of Justice is simjily a verification of Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson's statement. When the people of Canada come to understand this amendment of the Minister of Justice, they will see that it is simply a declaration that we have no hold upon the Grand Trunk Railway ; they can acquire that stock under any agreement they choose to make with the Grand Trunk Pacific Rail-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: way. They can say to the, Grand Trunk Pacific : We will give you terminal facilities at Montreal for your road for that stock. They can acquire it by such a bargain as that, and the people of this country could not force the Grand Trunk Railway to see that the Grand Trunk Pacific fulfilled its obligation in operating the road from Quebec to Moncton, a section which is practically uncalled for, and which will be of no benefit to the people of this country in transporting grain from the west to the Atlantic, because it cannot compete with any line now in existence or with the water route. What is the use of the government trying to make the people of this country believe they have got security, when they have not security ? If they want security, let them put in the word suggested by the leader of the opposition, which would bind the Grand Trunk to the amount of $25,000,000. If that is done, we will be satisfied that the Grand Trunk Railway will be in this scheme and of it, but if you put in the word suggested by the Minister of Justice, the Grand Trunk are not in it, are not of it, and are not responsible to the people of this 'country for one cent of money under that section.

One of the chief reasons given by the government for the construction of the eastern section of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway was that it would bring business to the ports of the maritime provinces. There are two ways of getting from our Canadian West to the Atlantic sea-board ; one is north of the great lakes and the other is south of them. Let us consider for a minute which of these ways of getting to the Atlantic sea-board the Grand Trunk Railway will take. The Grand Trunk Railway have improved their line from Chicago to Port Huron, and have double tracked it ; they have improved their line from Port Huron to Toronto, both by the Grand Trunk main line and by the western division ; they have improved their line from Toronto to Montreal by double tracking it, and at the present time they have one of the best roads on this continent. They have improved their line from Montreal to Portland so that it is now a first-class railway in every respect. The conditions of operating railways south of the great lakes, the climatic conditions, are much more favourable. The conditions with, regardi to the question of fuel are very much more favourable than they would be north of the lakes, much more than they are even on the Canadian Pacific Railway, which touches the great lakes where coal can be easily secured. But what about the coal needed to operate a railway 100 miles away from where it can be delivered to that road by water ? Then as I said, there are the climatic conditions to take into account. Now, what is the distance from Winnipeg to the Atlantic sea-board north of the lakes, and what is the distance from Winnipeg

south of the lakes by way of the old Grand Trunk system ? I contend that the Atlantic sea-board can be reached more easily south of the great lakes by way of their well developed line, owned for almost the whole distance by that company. The mileage will be less from Winnipeg to Portland than it will be fri m Winnipeg to St. John or Halifax via this northern route.
Will you give us that mileage ?
The mileage from Winnipeg to Portland will be a little over 1,800. I have not got the exact figures, but I calculate it will be a little over 1,800.
What is the other ?
Well, I calculate the distance from Winnipeg to Moncton will be about 1,900 miles ; then you add the distance from Moncton to St. John and from Moncton to Halifax by way of the Intercolonial.
What is it by the southern route ?

I stated that by the southern route, by way of Chicago to Portland, the distance will be a little over 1,800 miles. 1 stated that the mileage from Winnipeg to the Atlantic sea-board at Portland by way of Chicago would be less than the distance to the Atlantic sea-board at St. John or Halifax via the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. That is the view I take of it ; and I say that it is in the interest of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, which will practically control the Grand Trunk Pacific, to use the lines which they already have. That brings us to the question of the contract : In what way is the Grand Trunk Pacific bound to operate this eastern division ? In the amendment, as I understand it, the leader of the opposition desires that the Grand Trunk shall pay a reasonable sum, that it shall pay par for this common stock of $24,900,000 which it has to acquire. That is what the amendment of the leader of the opposition means. The government are willing that the Grand Trunk shall acquire that stock for a nominal sum, it may acquire it for $1 or 10 cents on the dollar. The fact of the matter is that the Grand Trunk will have control of this railway, and they will have very little interest in it if they acquire the stock for 10 cents on the dollar or 5 cents on the dollar ; but if they have to pay 100 cents on the dollar for the stock, they would have some real interest in the Grand Trunk Pacific. They are not going to have any very real interest in it because they are not going to pay very much for this stock, and that is the intention of the Bill.
At one o'clock, committee took recess.
Committee resumed at three o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose for recess we were considering to what extent the Grand Trunk Railway were interested in the Grand Trunk Pacific project. It has been shown that by the Grand Trunk Railway Company owning the common stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific to the amount of $24,900,000 it absolutely controls the policy of the Grand Trunk Pacific. There will be a board of directors for the Grand Trunk Pacific, but the directors will only hold proxies to vote in the way in which they are directed to vote through the influence of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. I pointed out that it would be in the interest of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, controlling the policy of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, to divert the traffic which the Grand Trunk Pacific gather in the North-west for transportation to the sea-board south of the great lakes instead of carrying it over the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway to the sea-board north of the great lakes by way of Quebec to St. John or Halifax. The reasons I gave for that were simply that the Grand Trunk Railway Company has improved its road-bed all the way from Chicago to Portland to such an extent that it can haul freight cheaper, and that it can thus get the earnings from carrying the freight all the way instqad of allowing it to pass over the government road. Then again the eastern section of the Grand Trunk Pacific will be finished last. It will be finished very many years after the Grand Trunk Pacific road and its branches are built in Manitoba and the North-west Territories. Therefore, for a number of years freight gathered by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway in Manitoba and the North-west will have to find its way to the sea-board and of necessity it cannot, even if the Grand Trunk Railway Company were willing, find its way out by the eastern section of this road. The question was raised as to what extent the Grand Trunk Pacific is bound to take its freight which originates in the west to the sea-board by the government portion of this road. I think I remember the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) saying that the Grand Trunk Pacific would under no consideration dare violate the spirit of this agreement, because the agreement was an agreement with the government of Canada. My own impression is that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, in years to come, when the influence and effect of this debate waste away and other men of this government,, or possibly of some other government, take office this obligation will not appear so strong as it may to-day, that there will be no moral obligation to observe and that the only obligation which will be observed will be that which is imposed by a strict interpretation by the contract in existence. Therefore, I do not see on what the hon. Minister of Finance and the hon. Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) can base

the assertion that this government, or any future government, would dare to bring pressure to bear upon the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway in any way in which the contract did not justify. It seems to me that history in this matter is repeating itself. A few years ago we had before us the project extending the Intercolonial Railway system to Montreal. That was advocated by the present administration and opposed by the opposition. What was the effect of the agreement ? AVhat did it bring about ? It brought about the extension of the Intercolonial Railway to Montreal. What else did it bring about ? It enabled the Grand Trunk Railway to do something which it had never done before. It enabled the Grand Trunk Railway to make Portland its summer terminal as well as its winter terminal. It had not developed Portland as far as its summer terminal was concerned, but through the tremendous advantages it got from the Drummond County Railway deal, through the rental it received, for the use of the line between Ste. Rosalie and Montreal and for the use of the Victoria bridge and in other ways it got sufficient money to enable it to improve its whole line to Portland and also to spend a considerable amount of money on its terminals in Portland. That was not contemplated by the government. That is not wThat the government thought the Grand Trunk Railway Companay were going to do, but that is what the Grand Trunk Railway Company did do and that is one of the effects of the bargain between the government and the Grand Trunk Railway Company in respect to the .Drummond County deal.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to draw your attention to your ruling this morning in connection with this subject. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Kemp) is not discussing the resolution before the committee. I understand your ruling this morning. was that discussion must be confined to the resolution before the committee. I ask for your ruling on the point of order.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: He is discussing the amendment.
He is not discussing the amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry that I was not in a position to hear the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kemp). I was trying to do a little work on the quiet. The hon. gentleman knows as well as any hon. member of the House that we all desire that each member shall keep to the subject.
The bargain for carrying the Intercolonial Railway to Montreal has nothing to do with this resolution.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member (Mr. Kemp) knows if he has been out Mr. KEMP.
of order, what the resolution is, and if he has really been discussing a question outside of that I will appeal to him to come to the question. But, I really did not hear him.

Mr. Chairman, I have the utmost respect for your ruling and I can assure you that I shall not depart from the rules of the House in such a way as to make it necessary for you to call me to order. I was just illustrating my argument by referring to a former bargain made by the government. What I said was that history was repeating itself in regard to this bargain, and in regard to the Bill which is now before us which will enable the Grand Trunk Railway Company to develop its whole line from Chicago to Portland, which will enable it to build up Portland and which will give the Grand Trunk Railway an outlet from the North-west by way of Chicago. That is something which I am sure the government did not intend when this bargain was made any more than that it intended that Portland should be built up by the Drummond County agreement. Yet I contend that is what is going to happen. Another thing that makes me very suspicious that the Grand Trunk Railway Company are not absolutely sincere in regard to operat: ing the eastern section of this road is the fact that there is no agreement between the Grand Trunk Pacific and the government in regard to terminals at St. John or Halifax or in regard to the use of the government road from Moncton to St. John or from Moncton to Halifax. Surely this is very important and if the Grand Trunk Railway had gone into the arrangement intending to utilize the Intercolonial Railway from Moncton to St. John or from Moncton to Halifax would there not have been some reference to it in the bargain. Under what clause of the agreement can the Grand Trunk Railway be compelled to build elevators and wharfs at St. John andi Halifax ? We have heard a great deal about the tremendous amount of money the Grand Trunk Railway Company is spending at Portland in terminal facilities. What amount of money are they willing to spend at these other places ?
