Surely, if the Grand Trunk were serious about this matter they would have had some agreement with the government in reference to it. Suppose that hereafter when the government say what they will charge the Grand Trunk as a rent for the use of the Intercolonial, the terminals at St. John and Halifax, could not the Grand Trunk refuse to pay the sum asked, and would not that be a loop-hole by which they could get out of their bargain ? I cannot help characterizing the whole contract as a very loosely drawn document indeed.

If it was the intention of the Grand Trunk to divert the traffic via Chicago, why should they originally have applied for a charter from North Bay for

900 miles of road, which would cost them $50,000,000 ?

The original proposition of the Grand Trunk Railway to make North Bay and Port Arthur their objective points, instead of Moncton, was a sane proposition. So far as building a line in the east was concerned, all that the Grand Trunk originally proposed was to build from North Bay or Gravenhurst, in order to connect their existing lines in eastern Canada with Port Arthur. Mr. Hayes, on November 24 last, stated in the ' Globe ' that they intended to buy the Canadian Northern Railway, and that was evidently their first intention. I am perfectly safe in saying that the Grand Trunk do not want this railway from Winnipeg to Moncton, which has been forced upon them.
If it is the intention of the Grand Trunk to divert the grain via Chicago, why did they apply for a charter from North Bay at all ?

The Grand Trunk were desirous of getting to the head of Lake Superior, but this proposed road takes them far to the north of Lake Superior. Let me call the attention of the House to this fact : the Canadian Northern Railway are now at Port Arthur, and the Canadian Pacific Railway at Fort William, and under an agreement with the Manitoba government the Canadian Northern Railway have reduced the rates on grain within the last few years, to the extent of 4 cents per hundred pounds.
That does not answer my question.

The Grand Trunk have a perfect right to ask for a charter to build to any point they please, and as a matter of fact in the Bill we have passed they have asked for a charter to the Yukon. In a contract like this, which the people of the country will have to spend vast sums of money to carry into effect, it seems to me that if the government intended that the Grand Trunk should carry grain to the head of the lakes, they should have inserted a clause in the charter providing that from Winnipeg and all corresponding points on the Canadian Northern Railway, the Grand Trunk should never charge higher freight rates than do the Canadian Northern Railway. The Canadian Pacific Railway are to-day charging 2 cents per bushel more than are the Canadian Northern Railway from Manitoba points. I am told that in time the Canadian Pacific Railway rates will come down, but they will only come down because of the competition of the Canadian Northern Railway.

The Canadian Northern Railway has a bargain with the government of Manitoba, whereby the people of Manitoba
agree to pay any shortage or any loss. That is a different proposition entirely.

I do not see that that has much bearing on the subject. The hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) will not deny that the people of the west are getting the benefit of a reduction of 4 cents per hundred pounds on grain carried on the Canadian Northern Railway, and if this government had at heart the welfare of the shippers and grain growers of the west, they would have provided in this contract that the Grand Trunk should carry freight at the same rate as the Canadian Northern Railway carries it. Let me point out, that there are two practical ways in which the Grand Trunk Railway might bind themselves to operate this eastern section. One way is, by purchasing the $24,900,000 of stock at par, which would make them absolutely interested in the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the other way is, that the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada should give a guarantee that the freight carried over the Grand Trunk Pacific, would not be diverted to American ports. The Minister of Justice admitted this morning that the only guarantee we have that the Grand Trunk will operate this eastern section, is a second mortgage on the five million dollars worth of rolling stock which is to be ear-marked for the eastern section. I would like to have the opinion of the Minister of Justice as to what that second mortgage is worth. As a matter of fact it is only worth the equity of the mortgage, and, what is that equity ? How could you realize on that second mortgage ? Suppose it should become necessary for the government to force the Grand Trunk to carry out its agreement, and suppose the government foreclosed that mortgage, who would buy the equity in that mortgage ? Would any man in this House or out of it pay five cents for that equity ? Even suppose any one did buy it, the rolling stock could not be taken away, because the first mortgager would have his lien on it. No man would invest a dollar in it in any shape or form.
But, Sir, what will the Grand Trunk Pacific Company care for any moral obligation ? These gentlemen, I admit, are respectable gentlemen, as respectable as any others ; they are well intentioned men ; but we have an illustration of the working of this contract in the case of the agreement between the government and the Grand Trunk Railway Company with respect to the Intercolonial Railway. The letter of that agreement is not being lived up to. The Grand Trunk Railway Company are no doubt trying to live up to it, according to its strict legal interpretation ; but there is a lawsuit going on at the present time between the government and the Grand Trunk Railway Company in regard to that portion of the agreement relating to the traffic of the Drummond Counties Railway. It was rather startling to the Premier this morning

to be told that Quebec was nearer to Portland than to St. John or Halifax. I am surprised that with all the information which the right hon. gentleman and his colleagues have had on this subject, this fact was not brought out before. The distance from Quebec to Portland is 31S miles, while the distance from Quebec to Halifax is said to be 580 miles ; so that when freight from the west reaches Quebec, especially in the winter time, it will be more economical to take it to Portland than to Halifax or St. John. Therefore we are justified in discussing the details of this contract and moving amendments to it ; and in order to safeguard the interests of the country, it seems to me that it is the duty of the government to adopt these amendments instead of voting them down by sheer force of majority.

The great interest of the maritime provinces in this road is unquestionably in having it operated so as to divert, as far as possible, all the traffic originating in the west to Quebec in the summer, and to maritime province ports in the winter. Unless- the Grand Trunk Railway Company have such a direct interest in the eastern division that it is of the utmost importance to them to make that portion of the road capable of earning a large revenue, I do not think the purpose which the government profess to have in this matter, and which the people of the lower provinces unquestionably have, can be served at all. The view of the people of the lower provinces can be recognized in the resolutions which have been passed by boards of trade and various public bodies in Halifax, Truro, and elsewhere. In every case, while not solicitous to have this road constructed, they are anxious, if it is constructed, that it should be built over such a route as will, as far as possible, guarantee that freight originating in the west and in the hands of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, should be carried to the sea-board over that road. The right hon the Prime Minister, in speaking of this particular feature of the transaction at an earlier stage of the session-in fact, before the Bill had been introduced as a government measure at all, and when it merely appeared as a Bill to incorporate the Grand Trunk Pacific Company-in fact, at an earlier period, when I think it was spoken of as a Bill to enable the Grand Trunk Railway Company to obtain access to the west-stated in his opinion, legislation alone would be useless; that it would be important to make such stipulations or regulations as would insure the diversion of traffic in the direction. The right hon. gentleman at that time laid down the proposition that in order to make the new road effective in that direction, it would be necessary to resort to a geographical condition ; that is to say, it would be necessary to place the line of the road so far Mr. KEMP.
north as to make it almost essential to the welfare and success of the road that the freight gathered on it should be taken to Quebec. Now, as nearly as we can judge at present, the line of the road, as finally decided upon, passing south of Lake Winnipeg and into the city of Winnipeg, will not fulfil that condition. We do not know exactly how far north that road may pass through Ontario and Quebec on its way to the city of Quebec ; but we know, in the first place, that the traffic to be gathered up by the Grand Trunk Pacific in the west will be brought into Winnipeg, where it will be affected by ail the forces which have a tendency to divert the export of grain away from Canadian winter ports to ports on the Atlantic coast of the United States. That port which is typical, which represents all the others, which represents most fully the fears which the people of Canada have that the trade of this country will be diverted to United States ports, is Portland. Not only is that port favourably situated for export, being comparatively near to Canadian points, being only 300 miles from Montreal and 318 miles from Quebec, as compared with the longer distances which separate Montreal and Quebec from St. John and Halifax, but we know that the Grand Trunk Railway Company have spent at that port something like $20,000,000 in important, well-developed, and no doubt convenient terminals ; so that there is every reason and inducement for the Grand Trunk Company, id the furtherance of its own business interests, to divert such traffic as the Grand Trunk Pacific may collect in the west, over its older system to Portland. Now, there might be, it seems to me, a course followed in carrying out this measure, which would 'make it to the interest of the Grand Trunk Railway Company to overlook the reasons which might influence it in favour of Portland, and more anxious to develop the trade of Quebec and St. John ; that would be by the Grand Trunk Railway Company acquiring a direct monetary interest in the road. The amendment offered by the hon. leader of the opposition is entirely in this direction. His suggestion is that the $25,000,000 of common stock in the Grand Trunk Pacific should not be a great block of stock which may be acquired at a nominal price or for nothing by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, but that it should be acquired by that company paying for it exactly what that stock is worth ; and every stock in a well-devised, well-considered and sound commercial institution is represented by par. It is held, on the other hand, that the Grand Trunk Railway Company should not be required to do this, but that they should guarantee bonds to a sufficient amount to pay for the construction of all that portion of the western division of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway which will not be provided for by the sale of bonds, guaranteed by the gov-

eminent of Canada. It seems to me that the railway would he much better financed if the Grand Trunk Company were to buy the stock at par and apply the $25,000,000 raised in that way to the construction of that road, rather than to get the stock at a nominal value or at no value at all, and provide for the construction of the western division by the sale of bonds, which would probably be sold considerably below par. We have constant complaints from gentle-ment representing western constituencies in this House of the evils of over capitalization.
We hear, session after session, assertions to the effect that in every case where a road is over-capitalized or financed in the usual manner by having large issues of bonds sold below par, with the result that the nominal capital does not represent the money actually put into the construction of the road, but represents large blocks of bonds or stocks in the hands of ostensible shareholders-in every such case the companies operating these various systems have to impose such tolls on the traffic as will give dividends on the excess of capitalization. Over and over again, gentlemen representing the western portion of Canada have insisted on the evils of over-capitalization, yet here we have in this contract a provision for the transfer of capital stock to the extent of $25,000,000 into the hands of certain shareholders, who may not have one million dollars invested in the road. Under the circumstances, it seems to me that the proposition of the leader of the opposition is entirely in the direction of preventing over-capitalization, and consequently preventing the evils of which the people complain. If the Grand Trunk Railway Company took this stock at par and built that road, the chances are that there would be absolutely no necessity whatever to issue a second set of bonds. There would be no second mortgage on the road, and the stock which the Grand Trunk Railway held on the road, and for which it paid par, would be represented by a property worth every dollar paid for it. If the Grand Trunk Railway paid $25,000,000 for $25,000,000 of stock, the only liability resting upon that capital stock would be that first issue of bonds, guaranteed by the government, and for which, in all probability, the public would pay par. The consequence would be that the company, through purchasing $25,000,000 stock at par, would own a property which would give full value for every dollar put into it. There would be, besides, this great advantage, that the road would not be over-capitalized, and it would be to the direct interest of the Grand Trunk Railway, which owned this $25,000,000, actually invested in the road, to divert every ton of traffic originating in the west over the line of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. Otherwise, there always must be the idea that the Grand Trunk Railway will have a
divided interest in this matter, that its chief interest will be in the development of the western portion of its system, and its secondary interest will lie in bringing all the traffic originating in that western portion to enrich its older system between Montreal and Portland. It seems to me inevitable that the interests of the Grand Trunk Railway in that case would be largely to use the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway as a feeder for its older system, and not for the purpose of developing the eastern division. Under these circumstances, you could not at all blame the Grand Trunk Railway ; but. unquestionably, the people of Canada will blame us. if we do not show ourselves quite as much awake to our interests as the Grand Trunk Railway are to theirs. We should guard against the possibility of defeat of the intention of the government by so shaping our legislation as to make it in the interest of the Granl Trunk Railway to develop and build up the traffic of the eastern section, not only by diverting to it the traffic front the west, but by aiding the work of colonization as rapidly as possible. If we make it the interest of the Grand Trunk Railway to make the eastern division an important part of their system, we will have done all we could do in order to guarantee that the purpose set forth in the preamble of the Bill shall be carried out. That purpose was amplified at great length by the First Minister, when introducing the Bill. He explained that the intention was not only to develop the trade of the west, but to divert it as largely as possible over the eastern division. As regards the western portion, no doubt it will be profitable, and no doubt, if the Grand Trunk Railway is not prepared to go on with its construction, other companies are ready to do so. This session, the Canadian Pacific Railway came before the Railway Committee with a proposal to build a line from Winnipeg to Edmonton, same 700 miles, parallel to the line undertaken by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, and they did not ask o-ne dollar's assistance. They merely asked to be allowed to build it. What was the result ? The result was. that the Canadian Pacific Railway were met in such a spirit and with such discouragement that they withdrew their Bill, and, practically, the parliament of Canada prevented the Canadian Pacific Railway from constructing that great work, which would have covered a large part of the teritory to be traversed by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, and the construction of which would not have cost the country a dollar.
If the Canadian Pacific Railway are so anxious to build, why do they not build the Kirkella line that runs over the same ground in the same direction ?
They are rapidly building that road. It was made clear before the committee that in respect of every one

of these guarantees, the company had complied with every condition exacted from them in the previous session hy the Railway Committee ; and if in any ease there was seemingly a little delay, It was because there had been difficulty in procuring steel rails.
Why do they want the other charter, when they cannot complete the two they have ?

There can be no doubt at all that if one company can build, another can. If the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway can build this road ,there can be no doubt that the Canadian Pacific Railway could quite as successfully build it. Other companies were perfectly ready to go into that territory and furnish all the railway accommodation needed, without any assistance. There can be no doubt about that fact, that there is no necessity to assist railway construction through the fertile plains of the west. My hon. friend who has interrputed me must know that the prospect of successful railway construction in these territories is sufficient to induce capitalists to go in and build these roads without assistance.
My hon. friend must be aware that that same country has been there for the last twenty years, and that there is no road through it yet. Surely, that is an answer to that statement.
I suppose it can be said that it has been there for a thousand or two thousand years.
It has been .settled for twenty years.

It may not have been settled so thickly as to justify railway construction through it to as great an extent as through other parts of the west. The most these companies can do is to meet the requirements of settlements as rapidly as they are justified in doing so. I have no doubt that there are people in the west who have settled so far in advance of railway accommodation that they are in need of railways, but such cases are being overtaken very rapidly by the existing companies. The Canadian Pacific Railway, to my own knowledge, are rapidly building branches reaching out to the settlements which require railway accommodation, and I have no doubt that wherever there is sufficient colonization to give promise of paying traffic to the road, that company is perfectly ready to extend the road. My point is, that this scheme must be considered in two different parts ; the western part will take care of itself absolutely, but the eastern part Is problematical and may not be built for a long time. We have at this time no idea as to when the surveys necessary for the building of that eastern section will be completed; we know nothing of the country through which

it will run, although we have a blue-book that gives some information. No one pretends that a trial line has been run over the country or that we can gather sufficient knowledge from reports of geological surveys, which are largely compiled from the results of canoe voyages, to justify 'the selection of a line. Many of these reports are made by officers who never went two miles from the streams on which they were travelling. The information given to the House by the blue-book is no doubt valuable and important, but still it is not sufficient to establish the fact that a line of railroad fulfilling the conditions laid dowm by the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) can be constructed in that country. That being the case, it seems to me that if we are to have a successful scheme of transportation, complete from the eastern to the western extremities of the Dominion, we must see to it that the company behind this scheme, the Grand Trunk Railway Company, shall have so direct and deep and important an interest in the financial burdens which will be entailed on some one in the construction and completion of this railway, as to make it to their interest to see that the traffic of the west is not only collected in the west, but is carried over the eastern division of the transcontinental road to Canadian ports in the east. The figures given by the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) show that if this road is to be a successful carrier of grain, it must carry it at prices never yet heard of in the history of railways. Even if they should carry thirty or forty million bushels, or should carry the whole crop of the west, they would do it at such prices as would leave to the company practically nothing whatever to be divided as dividends among the shareholders.
Might I remind my hon. friend that my statement was, that if it was necessary, they could carry the grain at such prices ?

The hon. gentleman is right. The figures he gave last night show the prices at which the grain could be carried without a loss ; but If work is to be done at prices which merely cover the cost of performing that work, it is clear that it is done without a profit, and if we make it compulsory that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway should carry this great volume of through-traffic over that road and must carry it at prices that will leave no profit, it becomes perfectly manifest that it will be essential to the continued success of that enterprise, to the continued solvency and operation of the road from year to year, that the company shall develop, in every way in its power, enterprises along the line, shall promote colonization and develop in that country a great local traffic, because they cannot hope, at the prices they will be able to charge, to secure enough revenue

from the carriage of grain and lumber to enable them to meet their obligations to the government. If we assume the cost of that road to be as low as It has been estimated by government speakers, there will be a liability attaching to every mile of the road of $840 per year. How is that to be earned ? It cannot be earned with through grain traffic ; and, therefore, if we are to ensure the success of this enterprise and fulfil the hopes that have been held out to the people of the lower provinces, we must frame this legislation in such a fashion that the Grand Trunk Kailway Company, which is constructing this road, will be compelled by force of circumstances and the necessities of their position to develop and divert all the traffic that comes into their possession over that read and consequently to develop every local industry along the line and to become a great colonization company. Therefore, it seems to me that the amendment offered by the hon. leader of the opposition should be adopted, as it would frame this legislation in such a way as to practically compel the Grand Trunk Railway to put the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway on a sound basis in the most economical fashion, and to give assistance to the construction of that road to the extent of $25,000,000 of their money. In that way we would have taken the most important step of all and secured the completion and operation of the road in such a way as to realize for the people of Canada those hopes which the right hon. the Prime Minister and the government must have had in view when they introduced the scheme.

I wish to say but one word in reply to some statements with reference to the prairie section. The hon. member (Mr. Bell) would lead the committee to believe that the Canadian Pacific Railway are prepared to build a road up through that section of country to be traversed by the Grand Trunk Pacific, without any money grant or assistance whatever. I wish to draw attention to this fact, that the Canadian Pacific Railway at the present time have in that country one branch, called the Manitoba and North-western, on which they are building very little. They have another branch line which traverses practically the same country for which a charter was asked, called the Kirkella branch, on which they are building very little. They have also another branch in the same district, called the Great North-west Central, 'on which I do not think they are building at all. Therefore, if the people of the west have to wait until the Canadian Pacific Railway were to build all these roads, they would have to wait some time. The hon, gentleman has not taken into consideration that what the people of the west are suffering from is that the Canadian Pacific Railway are not subject to government control of rates, that they charge excessive rates, and even if the Canadian Pacific Railway should I
build all these roads, still, so long as the main line is exempt from control of freight rates, the people of the west would get no relief and would be in the same position as they are at the present time.
Amendment to the amendment (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) agreed to.
On the section 7, as thus amended,

Before this section is carried, I desire to propose another amendment to it, which is somewhat along the lines of the one I have already moved, although it is more limited in its extent. I have already moved an amendment which the government did not see fit to accept, by which, if adopted, it would have been necessary for the Grand Trunk Railway Company to become bound by all the covenants, conditions and stipulations in the agreement contained, and which are therein made binding upon the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. In speaking to that amendment I mentioned several clauses of the agreement which I thought contained stipulations that ought to have been made binding upon the Grand Trunk Company. I mentioned clauses 42 and 43 which have particular relation to the diversion of traffic. The amendment which I now propose is one that is more especially limited to clauses 42 and 43 and is to the following effect :
That section 7 be amended by adding thereto the following subsection :-
Notwithstanding anything in this Act or in the said agreement contained, His Majesty the King acting as aforesaid, shall not be bound or obliged to perform, carry out or fulfil any of the covenants, conditions nr stipulations in' the said agreement contained on behalf of the Dominion of Canada, unless and until the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall have entered into an agreement with His Majesty the King acting as aforesaid, by which the said Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall covenant and agree as follows : That neither the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company nor the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall in any matter within its power, directly or indirectly, permit, advise or encourage the transportation of traffic by routes or at rates other than those provided in the said agreement, and that each of the said companies shall, in all respects and in good faith, use its utmost endeavours to fulfil the conditions upon which public aid is granted and accepted, namely, the development of trade through Canadian channels and to Canadian ocean ports.
That is an amendment which, I think, ought to commend itself to the government. In effect it amounts to this, that the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall be obliged to enter into a covenant with the government that neither tliei Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company nor the Grand Trunk Railway Company itself shall do anything to encourage the transportation of traffic otherwise than by Canadian routes, and further that both companies shall in all respects use their best endeavours to

fulfil the conditions named in the contract with regard to the transportation of traffic through Canadian routes. The reasons which might be adduced in support of this amendment I have gone over pretty fully already in support of the amendment 1 have already suggested. I do not want to go over them again with anything that might be regarded as unnecessary reiteration. I point out again the reasons to which I have adverted, regarding the diversion of the traffic to United States ports and by United States routes. I say that inasmuch as the Grand Trunk Railway of Canada is seeking aid in the construction of a line to the west, there is every reason why this amendment should be added to section 7, providing that the stipulations on behalf of the government shall not take effect until the Grand Trunk Railway shall have entered into the stipulations contained in this amendment.

I had hoped that this amendment might be accepted by the hon. gentlemen opposite. We have tried in various ways to obtain some provision in this Bill that might give a little security, to the country for the performance by the Grand Trunk Railway Company of what are considered by the government essential features of the arrangement. Perhaps the feature that interests the country more than any other is that which relates to the traffic to be carried by the railway called the great transcontinental railway. If there is no provision made that will be effective as to the routing of that traffic and as to the' rates upon that traffic, it would be better [DOT]that the money should be saved and that the country should enter into no obligations. The government, by introducing into the agreement provisions relating to the routing of that traffic through Canada, and the rates upon it, admit that these are very important considerations for the future of the country.
The question is whether in this contract there is effective provision to secure the benefit of the conditions which have been inserted in it. I have listened with a great deal of attention to the arguments of the hon. Minister of Justice and the hon. Minister of Finance and I fail to see that there is one point from first to last in which protection has been afforded against the opposing and separate interests of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. I desire to say a few words upon that point because I think it is of the utmost importance in considering what the government proposes to do for the Grand Trunk Pacific, to see whether we shall have as a return for the assistance some substantial guarantee from the company which is really getting the benefit of the aid. The hon. Minister of Justice tells us, as if it were something of importance in regard to this question, that the Grand Trunk Railway Company is guaranteeing 25 per cent of the cost of the western section. Well,

let us consider for a moment what the Grand Trunk Railway Company is guaranteeing. Is there an hon. gentleman in this House who has followed the proceedings on this Bill who doubts for a moment that the word ' Pacific ' is a mere fiction, that the real name of the company which is receiving this aid from the government is the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, that the other is a thing of straw put up to enable the Grand Trunk Railway Company to receive the benefit without entering into' any obligations under this Bill in return ? The hon. gentleman says that the Grand Trunk Railway Company is guaranteeing the bonds for one-quarter of the cost of the road. The Grand Trunk Railway Company is simply guaranteeing 25 per cent of the cost of its own road. It is the Grand Trunk's road as much as any property the Grand Trunk Railway possesses the moment this Bill passes and the agreement is entered /into. Does not every person know that from first to last, that from the notice which was published in the ' Gazette ' by the solicitor of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, from the day the officials of the Grand Trunk Railway Company appeared first in the Railway Committee to the present hour, there has been nothing but the Grand Trunk Railway connected with this transaction, and that in all the negotiations between the Prime Minister and the Grand Trunk Pacific no person has appeared in the name of the Grand Trunk Pacific who has not been a director or an official in some capacity of the Grand Trunk Railway Company ? That company has been in it from first to last and the Grand Trunk Pacific is a mere fiction, a statutory name given to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, because the latter company does not wish to be. direct party to this transaction. I do not wish to belittle the value of the Grand Trunk guarantee of these bonds even to the extent of 25 per cent. On this side of the House we are not disputing that. The hon. Minister of Justice seemed to place that question before the committee as if we were ignoring the value of the guarantee. We do not, but we object to exaggerating the value of dt. We object to any over-straining of the importance of its entering into that guarantee because it is simply guaranteeing something that is in its own interest and for its own benefit. The Grand Trunk Railway Company will receive great benefit from this western division as a feeder, and if it were entering into a contract with some other railway company for such a feeder as this it would be glad to give such a guarantee as is stipulated here and would never expect from that company a gift of the majority of its stock. As the Grand Trunk Railway Company is to receive enormous aid from the country, we ask that it shall give in return some adequate covenant and obligation to protect the country under the provisions of this agreement. We have asked for that in

different shapes. We have asked for a covenant from the Grand Trunk Railway Company, but hon. gentlemen say: No, you cannot have a covenant. You can have the covenant of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, a covenant that is absolutely worthless when you consider the mortgages and obligations into which it must enter under these arrangements. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway is bound by these arrangements to mortgage its railway up to the extent of the whole cost of the railway. It give a mortgage for 75 per cent of its cost connected with the government guarantee, and it gives a mortgage next in connection with the Grand Trunk Railway guarantee for the whole of the balance to complete the railway. Even its rolling stock is mortgaged to its full value. The covenant of that company would not be considered worth $1,000 by any bank in this Dominion, and yet that covenant is all we can get in connection with this transaction. Failing in getting a covenant from the Grand Trunk Company we have asked the government to make provision in regard to the common stock of the Pacific Company so that at least we shall have some security, but again we have been met with a refusal. We contend that the arrangement made by the government in regard to the common stock of this company virtually makes a present of $24,900,000 of common stock to the Grand Trunk Railway Company. The hon. Minister of Justice shows clearly enough that he treats it so, because the proposal that we have made that the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall subscribe for the common stock in the ordinary manner is carefully met by the hon. Minister of Justice by striking out the word ' subscribed ' and by putting in the word 'acquire.' He knows the distinction between the two words and he knows that the charter of the Grand Trunk Pacific enables the Grand Trunk Railway Company to acquire the stock without paying for it. Thus, we are deprived of the protection that we would have if the Grand Trunk Railway Company were obliged to subscribe for this stock. Under its charter the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company has power to give its common stock as paid up stock for rights and privileges, and in exchanging its common stock for rights and privileges, it has tlie right to deal with that stock upon its market value at the time. We have shown clearly enough that under the circumstances of this contract it will be absolutely impossible to fix any market value for it, that nobody can say what the market value is because the stock will never be put upon the market at all. We have under this arrangement a condition of things under which the same board will exist upon the Grand Trunk Pacific as will exist upon the Grand Trunk Railway and these two boards, being the same individuals, will meet together to make this 376
arrangement. The board of directors acting for the Pacific will value the common stock which is to be given in exchange for the privileges, and the same gentlemen acting for the Grand Trunk will value the privileges which are to be given in exchange for the common stock. The Minister of Finance tells us, that his anxiety is lest this common stock should be frittered away at a fictitious value by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. But, what more perfect means could he have devised, for its being so frittered away, than the very arrangement he has made. What more simple process could be invented for giving this $24,900,000 away at a fictitious value ?
If the Grand Trunk Pacific give away this stock for a fictitious value, how can they get money to fulfil their obligations ?

The Grand Trunk Pacific gets 100 cents on the dollar in bonds for the cost of its railway. What more does it want for that ? It gets $20,000,000 of preferred stock for the equipment. What more does it want for that ? If this common stock is paid for, the money would be in the treasury and it would not be necessary to issue all these bonds. But the mere fact that the Grand Trunk can get this $24,900,000 without paying a dollar for it, compels an issue of 100 cents on the dollar for the whole cost of the railway. You are loading this railway up with bonds, because the common stock is not paid for. That is the transaction. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Heyd) has heard the discussion time and again, and it is wonderful that he should ask such a question.
I wanted to be sure.
I hope you are sure now.
I am not.
You mean, you do not want to be sure.

What is there unfair in our asking that the Grand Trunk shall pay for that stock ? It does not mean that they shall be compelled to pay the money right away. When a man takes $100 worth of stock in a company he pays it up as the needs of the company require it, and if the Grand Trunk subscribe for $24,900,000 worth of stock it will not pay a dollar on that until the money is required for the needs of the company. Is not that perfectly clear ? No call could be made upon that stock except for the necessities of the company, and the Grand Trunk directors being the directors in the Pacific Company, can protect themselves against any unnecessary calls. But the importance to this country would be that the obligation to pay that stock up would remain, and if the Grand Trunk Pacific makes default in its obligations to the country, the right to make that call will be there and we can get



compensation. That is the distinction and nobody knows it better than the Minister of Justice. The Minister of Finance told ns that if we did not give this stock to the Grand Trunk, it might be frittered away at a fictitious value, but what is the difference between that, and putting it in the hands of the Grand Trunk without their paying a dollar on it ? It might as well be in any other hands so far as the country is concerned. We will suppose that there are branches to be built, instead of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company issuing heavy bonds, they could call on the holders of the stock to pay up, say 10 or 20 per cent, or whatever might be necessary. If that 10 per cent or 20 per cent is paid up, it will rank for dividend, but we object to all this stock ranking for dividend when the money never gees into the treasury. The government proposal loads the company up with watered stock. The Minister of Justice has urged that the Grand Trunk will have an interest in the success of the eastern division because the branch to North Bay will furnish its line through Ontario with traffic. That is a very important consideration, and it shows very clearly to my mind why it is of the utmost importance that the Grand Trunk Company, should be under direct obligation to the government. Let us suppose that the Grand Trunk does receive traffic from the Grandi Trunk Pacific at North Bay. What control from that moment has the Grand Trunk Pacific over the traffic which may be way-billed through ? The Grand Trunk would carry out the instructions of the way bill, wherever it may be to-Halifax, St. John, Portland or anywhere else. But what is more easy, in the carrying out of the business of these two corporations, than to bill every carload of traffic that comes from the west to the Grand Trunk at North Bay. at Montreal, or at Quebec ?
Would not the distance via North Bay be much longer than the distance via Quebec ?

I am dealing now with the remark of the Minister of Justice, that the fact that the Grand Trunk could get its traffic at North Bay gave it an interest in the Grand Trunk Pacific, inasmuch as it would afford traffic to be hauled over its Ontario and Quebec lines. I am pointing out why that illustrates the necessity of having control over the Grand Trunk with regard to all that traffic. Suppose that the Grand Trunk Railway receives traffic from the Grand Trunk Pacific, billed from Edmonton or Winnipeg to North Bay, Montreal or Quebec, it matters not which. The Grand Trunk can then re-bill that traffic to any port it pleases. It is the easiest thing in the world for the companies to arrange the matter in that way
But if the distance is longer, why should it do so ?
I am not going into the question of distance now at all. The hon. gentleman, I suppose, assumes that the traffic of the Grand Trunk Pacific is going to Quebec.
I assume that all the traffic is going the shortest distance, that is via Quebec, and there is no motive for it to go to Montreal.

I am willing to assume that it all goes to Quebec. The Minister of Justice represented that some of it would go to North Bay. Whether it goes via North Bay or Quebec, there is nothing to prevent the Grand Trunk Pacific sending all its through traffic to these points, there to be delivered to the Grand Trunk. The Grand Tunk could then forward it to its destination, either via Halifax, St. John or Portland. It could do the same if the traflic were shipped to it at Montreal. There is no provision in this contract to prevent the Grand Trunk sending to Portland all the traffic it receives at Quebec, and it would send it there if it could save money by saving a long haul. Yet the hon. gentleman says that he has the interest of the Grand Trunk in this agreement as a guarantee that the traffic will be sent to a Canadian port. The interest of the Grand Trunk will be to send the traffic to its own nearest port. I will again read the words of the amendment which is designed to meet such a case :
That neither the Grand Trunk Pacific nor the Grand Trunk Railway of Canada shall, in any matter within its power, directly -or indirectly, permit, advise or encourage the transportation of traffic by route's or ait rates other than those provided in the agreement.
We want hotli companies bound l>y that -not only the Grand Trunk Pacific, lmt the Grand Trunk. When it receives traffic at either of these points, we want it hound that the traffic shall go to a Canadian port. Under the agreement as it stands, the Grand Trunk can send every carload of the traffic to Portland. There is not a word in the agreement to prevent that. If the hon. gentleman, who lias the interests of the country at heart, can devise some provision by which the Grand Trunk Company ahull be obliged to send the traffic to a Canadian port, we shall he glad to have his assistance.
Your contention is, that the freight having once arrived at Quebec can be diverted by the Grand Trunk from St. John to Portland ?

What I say is, that it is quite possible, consistent with all the provisions of this agreement, for traffic coming from Edmonton. Brandon, Winnipeg or anywhere else in the west, to be consigned to the Grand Trunk at Quebec, and the moment the Grand Trunk receives it at Quebec, it will become the forwarder, and

It can send it wherever it pleases without breaking this agreement in doing so ; and the Grand Trunk Pacific Company will have complied with its part of the agreement also. We want both companies to be hound to send the traffic to a Canadian port. There is another feature of this agreement the keeping these two companies distinct, which is important, and which perhaps has not been considered ; that is, with reference to the division of rates between the two companies. It appears to have been assumed that this traffic must necessarily go the whole distance over Grand Trunk Pacific rails ; but that cannot be relied upon. The traffic will go just where it i;s in the interest of the Grand Trunk for it to go. There is no question that a large portion of the traffic originating on the Grand Trunk Pacific will go over both railways. All that goes to Buffalo-and that is a very large traffic which you cannot stop-will go partly by the Grand Trunk Pacific and partly by the Grand Trunk. When you come to the question whether the Grand Trunk Pacific is going to earn enough to pay its rent, whether it is to be freed from the payment of rent to the government because it does not earn it, it is a very important consideration to know what the division of rates between the two companies shall be. The Grand Trunk Company may make the division of rates between the two companies such that the Grand Trunk can take the cream and leave the skim milk for the Grand Trunk Pacific. There is no provision in the whole agreement protecting the country against arrangements between the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific whereby all the profit shall go to the former and the latter be worked at a loss.
I mention that incidentally to show that from first to last the question of the possibility of the Grand Trunk acting in its own interests, which may be adverse to the interests of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and adverse to the interest of the country, has never been considered in these negotiations. Now, Mr. Chairman, this resolution is a very mild one indeed. It is one which I think no person can reasonably object to. It simply provides that what has been contracted for in this agreement on the part of the Grand Trunk Pacific shall be honourably carried out by both companies.
Where is the trouble about the Grand Trunk Railway agreeing to it ? I would like the Minister of Justice to teli us in what respect the Grand Trunk Railway will have any difficulty whatever in preventing the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway doing anything contrary to the terms of this agreement. What trouble would there be on the part of the Grand Trunk Railway in undertaking an obligation, on behalf of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, either to do or not to do anything. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will be the Grand Trunk Company's railway, and the Grand Trunk I 376i
will only be agreeing for itself. The same board of directors will act for each company, the same officers will control the whole system. They are one company to all intents and purposes. Should the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway contract with this government to do a particular thing or not do it, the Grand Trunk is in a position to make it perform honourably what it has undertaken.

The issue between the parties,' Mr. Chairman, is as to whether the Grand Trunk Railway shall be compelled to carry out the declared policy of the government. At the time it launched this scheme, the government declared that it had made a good bargain with a responsible company, namely, the Grand Trunk Railway. It is evident that the Grand Trunk Railway is the sole beneficiary in this transaction. No one who will scan the provisions of the contract carefully, can come to any other conclusion than that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway is merely a figurehead, merely a company on paper. Large benefits are being conferred upon' the Grand Trunk Railway. A very substantial assistance is given it in the west, and also on the eastern branch, by allowing the company to have the use of that branch for seven years, and probably three years more, without paying anything; the government undertaking to build that portion of the line. During the last two or three days we have been endeavouring to get from the Grand Trunk something by way of return. Absolutely nothing is obtained from it now under this agreement. It is idle to speak of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway in this matter. There is no benefit, no return to Canada in any case for the benefits that are conferred by the government. We ask that the Grand Trunk Railway be made responsible for the obligations assumed by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. We are asking to have it provided in the contract that the Grand Trunk Railway shall not get $25,000,000 worth of stock in the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway for nothing, but shall pay for it. This is the only means by which the public can be protected with regard to the eastern division. We have it acknowledged by the Grant Trunk Pacific Railway that it will issue mortgage bonds for the twenty-five per cent of the cost of construction which the government does not supply ; and should this $25,000,000 worth of stock go into the hands of the Grand Trunk Railway without payment, another unfortunate result will be that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will have to borrow money on second or third mortgage bonds in order to equip the line with rolling stock to the extent of $20,000,000. The only security we have got will therefore be made worthless. For what cause ? Well, it is very difficult to suggest the cause without suggestng something uncompli-

mentary to the government. We are told both by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Justice that not a line of this agreement can be altered, that it must be either accepted or rejected as a whole.
I fail to see why, if we amend this Bill, we should not also modify the agreement so as to bring it in harmony with the Bill. I do not accept that proposition. In my opinion we have the right to alter the terms of the contract and to frame such an agreement as we believe to be fair and just. It will then be for the parties to the agreement to consent to the modifications or let the contract fall through. The only possible ground upon which the government can pretend that any benefit results to Canada from this contract is that the Grand Trunk Railway undertakes to guarantee the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway for the construction of the western division to the extent of 25 per cent of the cost. But does that confer any advantage on this country ? The construction of the western division is, to all intents and purposes, a private enterprise, wholly under the control of the Grand Trunk and Grand Trunk Pacific Railways.
Assume that we are not dealing with a transcontinental railway but that a railway is being constructed from Winnipeg to the Pacific ocean. We are guaranteeing it as largely as we ever do, we are guaranteeing it to an extent that is probably not necessary, having regard to the facility with which a railway can be constructed over the prairie. The Grand Trunk and. the1 Grand Trunk Pacific are identical, but} whether they are identical or not it is simply a case of a company undertaking to build a railway on condition that if we provide three-fourths of the money required they will provide the other one-fourth. Can in itself for one moment be said to be something done for Canada, in return for the concession we are making in the matter of this transcontinental railway ? If it were' that the Grand Trunk Rii^lway were coming to our aid in the construction of the eastern division, then perhaps a plausible argument could be advanced that this was something the Grand Trunk was doing in return for what we are doing by this contract. But this is in the construction of that portion of the railway which is to remain the property of the Grand Trunk Pacific from which we derive no more benefit than we do from that construction of a section of railway in any other part of Canada. It is impossible to point out how we are to obtain a return from the fact that the company are to contribute a certain portion of the money required to bui'ld their own line. I call the attention of the government to a fact- which will be significant to the minds of those to whom the government is ultimately responsible-namely that from the 30th of July, when this scheme was announced

Rivers Wilson adre,sse:d*that committee he made the remark that the old Grand Trunk Railway would stand behind this enterprise. We have not been content that they should stand behind it, we have required, and they have readily consented, that they shall be in it, and of it, . and form the whole thing.
That is pretty strong.
Who said that ?

The Minister of Finance, on the 12 th of August,- speaking on that question in this House. He went on :
W-e think it is to the advantage of this country to have the Grand Trunk Railway extended both east and west and we think it is better that (thus enterprise should toe in the hands of the old Grand Trunk Railway than of promoters who could be characterized as irrespon-slbles.
What is the hon. gentleman speaking of there ? He is speaking not of any scheme with which the Grand Trunk Company shall be remotely connected, but of a scheme by which the Grand Trunk Railway as it is in Canada to-day, shall be extended east and west, meaning-if the language istohaveany meaning at all-that we are to have the Grand Trunk Railway system extended into western Canada. I would like to ask you, Mr. Chairman, if this is tiie fact, what kind of a company are we dealing with in reference to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway ? This is a great scheme. It is not an ordinary transaction where we say to a company : We will give you a charter to build a railway. In that ease parliament very properly require that there shall be substantial people behind it, men who can put into the enterprise a sufficient amount of money to make it a success. But if this is important in the ease of an ordinary railway, how much more important it must be in a case such as this, where the government is entering into a gigantic scheme to construct the eastern division out of the money of the people of Canada, when, if it can be made a success at all, the whole success of the enterprise depends upon having men of undoubted ability and a company of undoubted substance at the back of it, to take over the railway when it is constructed, and to carry it on in a successful way to develop the trade resources of the country. Now, the hon. gentleman points out that we cannot expect that this Grand Trunk Pacific Company will be able to raise even the $5,000,000 that is to be paid in as a deposit, emphasizing still further the fact, which I think is becoming very evident to this House, that this Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company is a company only in name, and that the Grand Trunk Company, as has been pointed out by members of the government themselves, are the parties that the' government understood were launching this transaction and would consummate it through the medium of the government. The minister says that the Grand Trunk has declared its intention to be a truly
Canadian road. That is a matter of faith only, and we know that the road to a very bad place is paved with good intentions. I have referred to the Minister of Finance, I will now refer to the Minister of the Interior, although others have spoken in the same strain. The Minister of the Interior was speaking of what the leader of the opposition said in reference to having no security that the grain would be routed through Canadian channels, and in reply the minister said :
I may say that I agreed largely in -the view expressed by my hon. friend the Finance Minister, when he said that inasmuch as we were making a clear, distinct and unambiguous contract with -a responsible company, with a respectable institution which might reasonably be expected to -implement its -obligations, we should have a good deal of confidence that every reasonable effort would -be made by them to carry out the contract.
Referring back to wbat the Minister of Finance said, speaking of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, we see that the Minister of the Interior endorses the view that we are dealing with the Grand Trunk Railway Company. But he makes this absolutely clear when he says :
He (-the leader of the opposition) said that there was no s-a-ncti-on, no penalty provided in case the G-ran-d Trunk Rail-way -failed to meet Us obligations in that respect.
Did the Minister of the Interior at that time say that it was not with the Grand Trunk Railway Company we were dealing so far as the routing of traffic was concerned, or as regards the obligation to carry out the policy of the government of having an all-Canadian route over which grain would travel instead of feeding the railways of the United -States ? Did he say we were not dealing with the Grand Trunk Railway ? No ; he pointed out what the leader of the opposition understood at that time, namely, that we were dealing with the Grand Trunk Railway. Then he says :
But I go further, I would not coinsider it at all advisable -to put in this contract a final clause-a clause -that would provide, for instance, that a fine in the ordinary sense, should be levied against the Grand Trunk Railway for the violation of this clau-se.
Mark, Mr. Chairman, that here again the Minister of the Interior regarded it, as I venture to say every member of the government then regarded it-because I do not want to impute bad motives to them, but only that they have been over-matched by the Grand Trunk Railway Company-he regarded this contract then as being with the Grand Trunk Railway Company. He goes on further and says :
No parliament, certainly -not the parliament of Canada, was ever -asked to assent to an important fi-nia-n-cial proposition which w-a-s so buttressed with security, so im-pregnably fortified by all the securities that were required, as this proposition which we are dealing with at the

present time. Amd yet, w,e are asked to believe that after a little while the Grand Trunk will fail to carry ouit its contract and it won't go on. What does that argument amount to ? What is the Grand Trunk going into this scheme for ?
Well, I suppose we know pretty well wlmt they are going into the scheme for now :
It is because it has a magnificent system of railways in the eastern portion of Canada, because there is 'an enormous and growing traffic in the w-est, and the Grand Trunk wants to get there, and by means of this railway it is going to get in. Moreover, its thousands of miles of railway all over Canada are going to be connected with the growing trade in western Canada, and they are going to do a large and profitable business in consequence.
Then the hon. gentleman points out that they are going to make millions*of money out of it, that they are not going to abandon it. Summarized, it comes to this, that the government understood at the time, or If they did not so understand it they represented it to this House and to the people of Canada that they were getting the security of the Grand Trunk Railway, not in an isolated instance, but for the carrying out of the scheme as a whole ; they represented it as an extension of the Grand Trunk system, they represented it as a means by which the Grand Trunk was extending its system into the west, with connections in the east. Now, I charge it upon the government that, if at this stage, as they appear likely to do, they refuse every reasonable amendment which can be made, giving to the Grand Trunk all the profits of this great scheme, and while giving to them all the benefits, still refusing to ask the'Grand Trunk Railway Company to become responsible for the faithful carrying out of this contract, they are not acting I believe in harmony with the wishes of the people of Canada, nor in the interest of the people of Canada.

We have the very curious spectacle of the government endeavouring to avoid taking securities upon a property upon which it is quite competent for them to take security in the present position of affairs. The government profess to be anxious to build a transcontinental railway. For some reason or other they are undertaking to build the eastern portion of it, the expensive portion of it, that portion which we believe will not be a paying portion. We think that the prairie section of the line is a good business proposition. We believe that under ordinary conditions the government would find very many bodies of men who would undertake the building of that western section. Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann are duplicating that line in the west. We are contending that the security which the government is taking from the ' Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company for operating thie eastern section of the line is practically a second mortgage, because the Mr. LENNOX.
rolling stock is already mortgaged to the extent of $5,000,000. The Grand Trunk Pacific Company is authorized to mortgage its line to the amount of its full value and the government has the ordinary promise of the company to operate the road in addition to a second mortgage upon $5,000,000 rolling stock. The promise is practically valueless if the railway company does not find it in its own interest to live up to it. We are suggesting that the government should take security upon the western section to ensure the carrying out of the obligation that is undertaken by the Grain! Trunk Pacific Railway Company for the operation of the eastern section and that it should take such further securities as are outlined by this amendment. The government, instead of trying to get all the security it can, has apparently made up its mind to take as little security as possible.
I do not propose to go into the point made and so very clearly made by my hon. friend from East Toronto (Mr. Kemp) who showed that it would be in the interest of the Grand Trunk- Railway Company, when it gets to Winnipeg, to divert its traffic over its own line by way of Chicago. X believe that any railway man of experience would tell the minister that such would be the course most likely to be pursued by that company. Now, we have the unique spec-' tacle of the government endeavouring to avoid taking the security that it might take for the payment of interest upon nil expenditure of at least $100,000,000. When this matter comes to be worked out I think' it will be found that there was great necessity for having this security taken by the country. It might be taken for granted that the government under ordinary circumstances would be anxious to obtain all the security possible. Why has this line been divided into two sections ? Why does the government persist in refusing to take security by not retaining an interest in the western division to ensure the payment of interest on the money it is expending in building a portion of the line ? That in something I cannot understand, and I am quite sure that the government does .not realize the serious position that it will be in if it passes this Bill without including in it the amendments which have been offered.

Mr. Chairman, I am justified in discussing this matter at some little length. A few minutes ago one of the most intelligent, one of the brightest business men on the other side of the House and a gentleman of considerable importance in hi;? party, tlie lion, member for South Brant (Mr.' Ileyd), actually interrupted my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) and asked iny hon. friend for some information on this question. When he got his answer he said :	I wanted to know, showing that
there was something in this matter that

even that brig]it gentleman did not know. I think there are a great many hon. gentlemen, probably not quite as bright as that hon. gentleman, who also want to know, and I think there are a great many people in the country who want to know and who are seeking for information. I did a few minutes ago, hear several groans from the other side of the House, merely typical of the groans that will come from this whole country when this load is shoved uj)on it. We have had this matter discussed very carefully and with a great deal of learning by legal men on both sides of the House and I do think, that, when a business arrangement of this kind is under consideration, it is not out of the way that an ordinary business man should have a little to say in regard to it. We are dealing with a business institution. The Grand Trunk Railway Company is a business institution, a very shrewd one, and we would lave thought that the government would have joined with the opposition in its endeavour to make as good an arrangement with the Grand Trunk Railway Company as wan possible under the circumstances. Instead of doing that we find that the Grand Trunk Railway Company is being sheltered by the government and by its followers. Why should hon. gentlemen opposite be so solicit tous about making a good bargain for the Grand Trunk Railway Company and about preventing the Grand Trunk Railway from assuming responsibility to any extent? Why should there be any such anxiety to protect the Grand Trunk Railway Company ? Have these hon. gentlemen become responsible to the Grand Trunk Railway Company in such a way to prevent them from asking for better terms for the country ? All the provinces of this Dominion have come up and asked for better terms. Why should we not urge upon the government that it should try to get better terms in the interest of the country ? All we are asking by this amendment to clause 7 is that the Grand Trunk Railway Company should do what the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, its own child, has promised that it will get it to do ; that is to stand behind it to the fullest possible extent in the work which it has to do. The right hon. Prime Minister led the country to believe that the Grand Trunk Railway was going to do that, that the Grand Trunk Railway was not only in it but of it, in fact, that it was the whole company. Under these circumstances I think it is most unreasonable that the government shall not insist that the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall assume some responsibility for the carrying out of this contract.
I believe the government has the verbal promise of the officials of the Grand Trunk Railway that the company will be behind the enterprise, and that it will be to its interest to back the Grand Trunk Pacific up in every way possible. This is just like going into a bank and saying that you will
back a man's note. The banker turns it up and says : Well, sign. All we ask the Grand Trunk Railway Company to do is to implement its promise. I could understand irresponsible promoters trying to evade responsibility. The eyes of the people of this country, and not only of the people of this country but the people of the old country, are upon this parliament and upon this Bill to-day. When you go into the financial circles of the old country they will investigate this matter because Sir Charles Rivers-Wil-son stated to his directors that lie was not going to make the Grand Trunk Railway Company responsible for one dollar. Yet, here it is stated that the Grand Trunk Railway Company is behind this scheme and responsible for it. Therefore, I contend it would have been better if we had had irresponsible promoters in this country to deal with because we would have known how to deal with them. I think it is an extraordinary thing that this whole discussion is allowed to proceed on this side of the House and that outside of twro hon. gentlemen connected with the government and of a question asked now and again wre have had no statement and no information from the other side of the House.
The country is calling for it. You have the majority, and you know it; and you can shove this thing through by merely saying aye. I certainly apologize to my hon. friend if I misunderstood him in any way. I gave his remarks exactly as I comprehended them. I do.

Well, I would like to point out to my hon. friend that all this amendment does is this :[DOT] It provides that:
The Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall not, in any matter within its power, directly or indirectly permit, advise or encourage the transportation of traffic by routes or at rates other than as provided in the said agreement, and shall in all respects and in good faith use its utmost endeavours to fulfil the conditions upon which public aid is granted and accepted, namely, the development of trade through Canadian channels and through Canadian ocean ports.
My hon. friend, perhaps, has not observed closely the provisions of the amendment. It comprises exactly the provisions to which he attaches so much importance. Why does he regard them of importance when applied to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, and absolutely of no importance when applied to the Grand Trunk Railway, which has its terminal in Portland and has every inducement to take its traffic to that port ?

I shall answer my hon. friend. There must be a management of this road which will be bound by the terms of the contract, and I care not what that management may be. But my objection is this, that hon. gentlemen opposite, whose aim it is to defeat this measure, are striving, in default of being able to do so, to obstruct its passage in every possible way. Their amendments are simply intended to cause delay. I can see no advantage, no additional safety, in what they propose, but I can see cause for delay in the construction of the work ; and as I consider the contract perfectly satisfactory in its present shape, I can see no reason why it should not go through. I hope I have made my objection plain.
Not by any means. Would my hon. friend be good enough to explain why a covenant with the Grand Trunk Railway would delay the construction of the work ?
I suppose the Grand Trunk Railway would have to be consulted.

When I entered the House a few minutes ago, my hou. friend the Minister of Customs was amusing himself and the House by a reference to the employees of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. He seemed to think that they would be an independent body altogether, absolutely free from the influence of the Grand Trunk Railway, and bound to carry out the covenants of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. That is theoretically quite correct, but I shall be very pleased to give the hon. gentleman some information how that works out practically and I can give him a parallel case in every particular.
You admit that I am theoretically correct.

Yes, but an ounce of fact is worth a ton of your theories. The Grand Trunk Railway is going to guarantee some bonds on this Grand Trunk Pacific Railway road, and is going to have a majority of the stock and control the hoard. The hon. gentleman thinks that the Grand Trunk Railway will not be the masters of the employees on that road. Let me point him to another case, to show him how that will work out. The Grand Trunk Railway guaranteed by traffic arrangement the bonds of the Chicago and the Grand Trunk Railway. The Chicago and Grand Trunk was under a distinct charter, just as distinct as that of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. It had a distinct board, but that board was composed partly of Gi-and Trunk Railway officials and directors. It had some independent directors, and was worked under an independent charter. In fact it had a charter from two different states. Yet in the practical operation the general manager of the Chicago and Grand Trunk Railway was appointed by the general manager of the Grand Trunk Railway. Not merely the station agents but the general manager and the traffic manager and every officer of the departments was appointed by the general manager of the Grand Trunk Railway, and every large transaction of the Chicago and Grand Trunk was reported directly to the Grand Trunk Railway at Montreal. It will be just the same with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway.
Were they able to violate their agreement ?

They did not violate agreements. They did what they thought was in the interests of their employers. The Chicago and Grand Trunk Railway gen-

eral manager, Mr. Spicer, was appointed by the general manager of the Grand Trunk Railway. He reported to the general manager of the Grand Trunk Railway. Of course, he sent in official reports'to his board, but the business was done in accord with the manager of the Grand Trunk hour by hour and day by day. In every considerable transaction he was in communication with the office at Montreal, and that gentleman's officers dared not make an important freight or other contract against the wishes of the general manager of the Grand Trunk Railway at Montreal.
Where is the parallel ? Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that this management can violate this agreement without any legal recourse on the part of the government or the shippers ?
The hon. gentleman asked whether the employees of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will be the employees virtually of the Grand Trunk Railway. That is what I asserted, and what he denied.
Supposing they are, can they violate this contract ?
They need not openly violate it.
Give an answer as a lawyer.

I explained that before, and the hon. gentleman knows it very well ; but there seem to be other gentlemen who do not. When a shipper comes to a station agent on the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, that agent will not say to him that the company is under obligation to send freight to Halifax or St. John. If the shipper happens to say that he wants to send it to Halifax or St. John, the agent will say, for instance, certainly you can ; there will be a steamer there next week, there will be an earlier one at Portland.
But suppose the shipper says nothing ?
Then it will go just where the agent wants, and that will be to Portland.

My hon. friend has now got on to another quibble. He says that the agent will tell the shipper that he can send the freight to Halifax or St. John, and there will be a steamer there the next week. But is he not aware of a clause of the contract which provides :
The company shall arrange for and provide, either by purchase, charter or otherwise, shipping connections upon both the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, sufficient in tonnage and In number of isallings to take care of and (transport all its traffic, both inward and outward, at such ocean ports within Canada, upon the said line of railway, or upon the dine of the Intercolonial Railway, as may be agreed upon from time to 3774
time, and the company shall not divert, or, so far as it can lawfully prevent permit to be diverted, to ports outside of Canada any traffic which it can lawfully influence or control, upon the ground that there is not a sufficient amount of shipping to transport such traffic from or to such Canadian ocean ports.
Yet he talks about the agent saying to this man :	You can ship by Halifax, but
there will be no steamer there for a week, and that is the hon. and legal gentleman who undertakes to dispose of a layman's criticism of the contract. I would prefer to take my judgment of it than his.
What is the hon. gentleman's objection ? We are providing that the Grand Trunk Railway shall be bound to do what he says the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway are going to do ?
As I said before the objection I have to these amendments is that when we have here a contract, the best ever made In this country
Oh, oh.

Yes. I repeat it, when we see hon. gentlemen opposite doing their best to destroy this scheme, to vote it down, and introducing amendments, I cannot help thinking-although I do not want to be uncharitable-that their object is to prevent or delay the progress of this great work.

The childlike simplicity and faith of the Minister of Customs is something that is absolutely refreshing. Here is a man who throughout his political life lias denounced corporations ; since I have come into the House I have head him denounce them ; he has no faith in railways or their pledges, now in Indignant tones, in the old fashioned thunder, he says : You have dared to doubt the faith of this railway baby of ours ! Why it is heresy to think that the men who have given their word in this bargain will not carry out their contract absolutely to the letter. He is so sensitive iu regard to the honour of these men that he absolutely refuses to have them bound by pen and Ink and paper, he will not have it, it would be an insult to tilts grand corporation, to the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk Railway, to doubt for a moment that they will not for all time, carry out the spirit of their contract. He tries to draw red herrings across the path and says that every one hailed with delight the prospect of the entrance of the Grand Trunk into Manitoba. We all bailed that with pleasure. We thought it would be to the advantage of Canada, of Ontario and of the North-west that the Grand Trunk should get an entrance into the North-west Territories and when the Grand Trunk proposed to build from North Bay to the west, when they were asking government aid which they always thought might, to a certain extent, be given to them, every man on this

side of the House agreed that it was a good thing to do. The government has seen lit to grant to the Grand Trunk Pacific aid to an enormous extent and to extend the road to the east. The only object of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House is to endeavour to secure a guarantee that the Grand Trunk Pacific whose childlike simplicity the hon. Minister of Customs so loudly proclaims, are going to carry out a verbal agreement. The Grand Trunk Railway are not bound by this agreement.
Mr. I1EYD. Why should the Canadian Pacific Railway also enter into this agreement ?
What has the Canadian Pacific Railway to do with it ?
Why cannot they get control of the officers of this railway and divert traffic over the Canadian Pacific Railway just as well as the Grand Trunk Railway can V
Now I did give credit to the hon. member for South Brant for having some business sense. He asks, why does not the Canadian Pacific Railway get possession of this road, get control of the rates.
I did not say that.
They do not pay the employees.
Why could they not get control of the officials and have the traffic diverted over the Canadian Pacific Railway as well as the Grand Trunk Railway can do it ?
The Grand Trunk Railway are getting the stock of this road for nothing.
That does not affect the question.

Well the question is too silly to answer. The New York Central Railway to-day, in this way and in this way only, owns the Canada Southern Railway, the Michigan Central Railway and the West Shore Railway.
What has that to do with this agreement ?

It is exactly similar to it, because they entirely control the employees. The Grand Trunk Railway Company are the men who will appoint the officials of the Grand Trunk Pacific and will pay them and they will control every ounce of business originating on the whole of this road through these employees.
