Suppose a shipper in Edmonton wants to send grain to England. He goes to the agent in Edmonton and gets a rate, we will say the same rate to Portland as to St. John. The agent at Edmonton says : We have the same rate to St. John, but it will be a day shorter going
to Portland as there are better shipping facilities there. The hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) is business man enough to know exactly what would happen and what will happen. It is the direct interest of the Grand Trunk Railway to send all of this traffic to Portland, because they get the same rate for hauling it practically the same distance from Quebec, but by taking it to Portland they get the whole of the terminal charges and in the other case they have to divide with the Intercolonial Kailway the proportion of the rate on 186 miles to Halifax and on something like 89 miles to St. John. Now it is not in human nature, it is not in business nature, not to take that advantage and every bushel of grain, every consignment of freight will go to Portland and not to St. John or Halifax unless the shipper distinctly says : I want this sent by such and such a port. Well, now the shipper is not a fool. He will take the route that the agent advises him to take. He will take the route where he can get the quickest service, where he is certain of vessels and of having the grain delivered promptly. The Grand Trunk Railway can delay a shipment if it goes to Halifax, and there is nothing in this contract that will impose a penalty on them for doing so. It is to their interest to send this grain to Portland if it originates at Edmonton andl they will send it to Portland without any doubt. Further, we believe, I personally believe, that it is the interest of the Grand Trunk Railway when that grain gets to Winnipeg in the winter time to send it via Chicago, because, as a matter of fact, the Grand Trunk Railway Company have within a comparatively few miles a connection from Chicago to Winnipeg. They own the line to Chicago and practically control the line up to Minneapolis and they can very easily make an arrangement with one of the roads there because there are spare roads from St. Paul to Winnipeg. I believe the grain and the trade will come that way because the Grand Trunk Railway now work in close connection with the Great Northern Railway and ship very largely to the British Columbia coast over the Great Northern.
Has my hon. friend with him the mileage of the connection between Winnipeg and Portland via Chicago, the Grand: Trunk Railway from Chicago to Port Huron and from Port Huron to Portland ?
No, I have not that.
I venture to say that if he would give the mileage It would be sufficient to disprove his statements.

I say the shipment of freight is being made to-day in that way from Ontario, via Chicago by the Great Northern Railway out to the Pacific coast notwithstanding your mileage. That is being done to-day to a considerable extent, and I

say that the danger is that when the Grand Trunk Railway get to North Bay, as I hope they will, they will not send any freight over the Grand Trunk Pacific. Now the point that we make, and X think it has not been disputed at all, is that the government have practically no security whatever that the Grand Trunk Railway will operate the eastern section of the line If It will pay them to give it up. The government have a second mortgage on $5,000,000 worth of rolling stock upon which there is also a first mortgage of $5,000,000. That is the only security except what is practically a note of hand that will take rank after all the other securities and which we all know will never be enforced. Now what we contend is that the government are in duty bound, if they go into this expenditure, to make the security for the operation of the eastern section as strong as it can be. We contend that the government should have the security upon the western section. I believe that the western section will be to the Grand Trunk Railway or any railway that builds or operates it a very paying proposition. Why should the government build and own and have the responsibility of the eastern section which some of us think will not pay ?
Why should the government build that and take the responsibility of it, why should they not take control over the section which will pay to an enormous extent on the prairies ? The Minister of Customs answers that by saying: The Grand Trunk won't do it, we cannot alter the contract. I am sure the Minister of Customs is right, the Grand Trunk will not come under any such obligations. They will not admit the liability under the contract of the cost of operating and paying interest on the eastern section. If this road is to be built for the benefit of Canada throughout, we ought to have all the safeguards possible, we ought to bind the Grand Trunk as tightly as we can, so that it will operate the eastern section, bad as the bargain is. so that they will send all the produce of the west over that road. We contend, and the argument has not been refuted, that the government are taking no security whatever, and that the Grand Trunk Railway is not under any obligation to pay the rent and operate that road, but that it will pay them better to drop it at Winnipeg after they get the prairie section built. Now, the whole question is very much on a par with the man who is doing business in his wife's name. The Grand Trunk Pacific is the wife of, the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and the Grand Trunk Railway Company is not liable for the debts of the Grand Trunk Pacific; the Grand Trunk is simply doing business, and is obtaining all this advantage from the Dominion government without, as we contend, giving any satisfactory security that they on their part will carry out their bargain. The government, instead of trying to
strengthen their agreement iu every possible way, simply say: We have made these arrangements and we are not going to change them. Why? Solely because we have got the Grand Trunk Railway Company to go, in this matter of a guarantee, as far as they will go. The Grand Trunk know perfectly well what are the risks of undertaking to operate this road in the north, and making their connections with Quebec, with Montreal, with Toronto. They know perfectly well that if they should go as far as Quebec, it will pay them better to send all their stuff from Quebec to Portland-because they then get the whole of the earnings upon it-rather than send it to Halifax or St. John. Now, the opposition are arguing, not against this road, but that if you go into an expenditure of $100,000,000 or $150,000,000, every safeguard possible should be taken to secure trade for our own Canadian ports. That is our contention, and it has not been refuted, except by the very childlike simplicity of the arguments of the Minister of Customs who believes in the promises of the railway. We have nothing whatever to rely upon, we have no other security. Now, when the railway men were being examined before the Interstate Commission, one gentleman gave evidence which was significant. I think he exaggerated a little, at all events, he was speaking of American railways. He said that, taking all these men who owned railways and controlled them, individually he would believe any word that they said, he would take the word of any one of them for all they were worth in any transaction; but take them collectively as a railway corporation he would not trust them unless they were under seal, and under such control that the state courts could make them do it. Now I do not go so far as that, but I say that the Minister of Customs knows what human nature is, and he knows that whatever patriotism the Grand Trunk people may have now, whatever patriotism he may have, if he is shipping large quantities of stuff, he will send it by the way that suits him best. I say that now is the only time for the government to make such conditions and stipulations in this contract as will, as far as possible, ensure the building up of our own maritime province ports of St. John and Halifax, and possibly other ports that may be opened up. But if he allows this contract to go as it is now, he has no security whatever that these shipments wifi go through Canadian ports. Clause 45, which the Minister of Customs has so strongly emphasized, says:
The company shall arrange for and provide, either by purchase, charter or otherwise.
Now, ' otherwise ' covers a great variety of ways, they may charter from time to time vessels to carry their stuff; they know beforehand what stuff they will send there, and they may divert it to Portland just as easily as they could send it to St. John or

to Halifax. But they will earn more on their money if they send the freight by Portland, and the Minister of Customs does not for a moment believe that it is a business proposition to say that these men, in their present contract, have said that they will always be patriotic and send their freight to a port in Canada, when in five years not one of these men may be in control of the Grand Trunk or of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and it will be to the interest of that road to send all their stuff to Portland, as under this contract I am perfectly certain they will do.

It is very refreshing to hear the director of a railway corporation charging the Minister of Customs with childlike simplicity because he believes the word of a railway corporation. The hon. gentleman no doubt knows whereof he speaks. I have more faith in the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, even than he would lead us to believe they deserve. Now, Mr. Chairman, it is also refreshing to hear our friends opposite become so zealous about the ports of the maritime provinces. Why, the echoes of their voices have scarcely ceased ringing in this chamber when they derided the very idea of building from Quebec to Moncton. Why, Sir, the soul of my hon. friend from Centre Toronto (Mr. Osier) burned with indignation at the idea of squandering the money of this country upon a road from Quebec to Moncton. His opinion was seconded by nearly every member on that side of the House, particularly by the member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker). If it is a waste of money to build this road from Quebec to Moncton, what are we to think of the efforts of the hon. gentlemen when they talked about ruining the Intercolonial by the construction of this new road? We said to them: We want to build this road from Quebec to Moncton because it will shorten the distance first, and secondly, because it will give the Grand Trunk Pacific an interest in the maritime provinces, which will be a strong inducement for them to use the ports in the maritime provinces. But the hon. gentlemen opposite tabooed this idea, and said we must use the Intercolonial. Well, their conversion has not come any too soon. They know they have got to face the electorate within the next two years on this question, and it is about time that they should begin to be converted. The only government of the Conservative party that is appealing for the support of the electors of any part of Canada on this question, is the Conservative government of British Columbia, and they are supporting the Grand Trunk Pacific scheme, and I would not be surprised if these hon. gentlemen opposite, when they come to face the electors, are also foundl supporting this Grand Trunk Pacific as one of the greatest schemes ever undertaken for the benefit of Canada.

Now, what is all this tempest in the teapot about? The hon. leader of the opposition desired that we should force the Grand Trunk Railway Company to route its freight by Canadian ports. If the Grand Trunk Railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific are one and the same institution, then, it will not be in the interest of the Grand Trunk Railway to divert the freight from the Grand Trunk) Pacific Railway. If, for instance, a shipment of grain is at Edmonton to be shipped to Liverpool and if the Grand Trunk Railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific are the same institution why should the Grand Trunk Railway have an official there to divert the trade from the Grand Trunk Pacific to some connection down by way of Chicago or North Bay to Portland ? If they are the same institution is it not in the interest of the Grand Trunk Railway that freight should travel over the Grand Trunk Pacific to the city of Moncton ? The only advantage, admitting that they are the same institution, that would accrue to the Grand Trunk Railway from diverting the trade to Portland would be that they would get a haul of 400 miles farther between Quebec and Portland than between Quebec and St. John. In other words hon. gentlemen contend that they are going to keep an army of servants and officials in the North-west Territories to go round amongst shippers and endeavour to divert the trade of that country to Portland for the purpose of getting the advantage of 100 miles of a haul from Quebec to Portland.
In violation of their agreement.
In practical violation of their agreement.
Whose agreement ?

In practical violation of their agreement if they are one and the same institution. If they are not the same institution, if they are distinct institutions, why should we force the Grand Trunk Pacific any more than, we force the Canadian Pacific or the Canadian Northern Railway ? For instance, if they are to be distinct institutions this case might arise : A man has a shipment of grain at Edmonton. A Grand Trunk Railway official comes along to him and says :	I want you to ship this grain
via the Grand Trunk to Portland. We will give you a lower rate if you will do so. What is going to prevent the Canadian Pacific Railway from coming along and say- [DOT] ing : If you will ship your grain from this point to the first junction with the Canadian Pacific Railway and thence by our line to Montreal, we will give you a lesser rate ?
If we are going to bind one company why not bind another company, if they are to be distinct institutions ? It seems to me that this is not a fair prop<r ition and will not

commend itself to the country. I am sure that the country -will be glad at last to know that these hon. gentlemen have become so zealous in defence of the maritime province ports, that, after fighting a proposition to build a line from Quebec to Moncton tooth and nail, they now come down and say : We must force this Grand Trunk Railway to ship their goods to Moncton because we are afraid, forsooth that they are going to keep a whole army of officials in the North-west to go round amongst the farmers and shippers of grain and try to seduce them away from their loyalty to their own country and send their goods by American ports.

The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Logan) aska if an army of officials is going to be employed by the Grand Trunk Railway to go around amongst the farmers and shippers of the North-west to seduce them, as he puts it, to ship their goods by American ports. It is not necessary for these officials to go around amongst the farmers because the farmers, when routing their grain, come to the officials and the officials do not go to the farmers.
Come to what officials V
Come to the Grand Trunk Railway station agents to ship their goods.
What officials will they come to-the Grand Trunk Railway or the Grand Trunk Pacific ?
They will interview the Grand Trunk Pacific officials appointed and controlled by the Grand Trunk Railway.
I do not care who controls or appoints them. They are Grand Trunk Pacific agents and if they influence a man to ship his goods by American ports they are violating this agreement.

The hon. gentleman says that he cares not who has the appointing of these officials. It makes a very considerable difference as to whether they are appointed and controlled by the Grand Trunk, Pacific or by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, because it makes a difference as to whose orders they will obey, whether they will obey the orders of the Grand Trunk Railway or the Grand Trunk Pacific which is only the shadow of the Grand Trunk Railway.

The argument of the hon. gentleman opposite is that these Grand Trunk Pacific officials will desire to divert the trade to the Grand Trunk Railway. Suppose they acted in accordance with that desire, would it not be a violation of the express terms of this contract ? It makes no difference who appoints them so long as they are officers of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway.

Well, now, I gave my hon. friend credit for far more astuteness than that. It is a simple matter to evade a thing of that sort. A little hint dropped into the ear of a shipper of grain will ac' complish the purpose they have in view without doing anything that will lay them open to the charge of having violated the contract. The hon. gentleman has made a statement that it is very refreshing to see hon. members who opposed the building of this eastern division of the line now endeavouring to have it fixed in the contract that all the freight should go by that eastern division. AVhy should the hon. gentleman be surprised ? If the government has determined upon its mad course, if it has determined to discard the Intercolonial Railway, it is the duty of this opposition and of every hon. member in this House to do his best to see that the interests of the country are protected and that the interests of the people who have to pay for this $100,000,000 are safeguarded.
May I ask the hon. gentleman if he is opposed to the building of this short line between Moncton and Quebec.

I am not afraid to answer the question. I come from the maritime provinces and I propose to try for re-election in the province to which I belong. I say here and now that I am opposed to the building of this eastern division and that I am prepared to defend the position that I have taken upon any platform in my own province. I would be only too happy to have the hon. gentleman come into my county and oppose me on the stump.
Come into mine. I have a better county.
The hon. gentleman's friends have been so kind to me as to give me another county and my constituency has been made so large that it will probably take me most of my time to attend to it.
I think so.

Very well : we will see what the results will be. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Logan) said that only one Conservative government, the government of British Columbia, had appealed to the people since the Grand Trunk Pacific scheme was proposed, and he said that the government of British Columbia were in favour of it. The hon. gentleman cannot show a single utterance by any public man on the Conservative side in British Columbia, favouring the government scheme, since the leader of the opposition made his proposal.
If the reports in the Liberal and Conservative newspapers alike are correct, the Prime Minister of British Columbia favour's the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific.

That is not the point. I say that since the leader of the opposition laid down his proposal, there cannot be found the utterance of any Conservative public man in British Codumbia, favouring the government scheme as against the scheme of the leader of the opposition.

At the opening of the campaign in New Westminster one week ago, the ' Daily Columbian ' reports Premier MacBride as saying, that the province of British Columbia was now getting the Grand Trunk Pacific without it costing the province anything, and he is claiming credit to himself for that.

What has that to do with it ?
Some lion. MEMBERS. Oh.

Just wait a moment please. These gentlemen opposite have had a very hard day of it, and they are anxious for a chance to laugh, just as a drowning man catches at a straw. They will find that this is a very weak straw for them. The hon. member says that Premier MacBride endorsed the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific through British Columbia, but is not the building of that western division of the Grand Trunk Pacific entirely in accord with a proposition of the leader of the opposition ? What we are talking about here is the building of the eastern division, and I defy my hon. friend (Mr. Macphersou) to point to any utterance of Premier MacBride or any other Conservative, favouring that. Let me deal with the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan).
Now you'll catch it.
Is the hon. member for Saskatchewan asking a question ?
No.

Then you had better hold your tongue, and keep still. Let me tell the hon. member for Cumberland, that the only Conservative government which has appealed to the people since the Grand Trunk Pacific scheme has been launched, is the Conservative government of Manitoba, and the Prime Minister of Manitoba denounced this scheme, and his party were so triumphant that the opposition were practically swept out of existence. I need not say that so far as the eastern division is concerned, the province of Manitoba is more deeply interested in it than the province of British Columbia can possibly be.
The Manitoba elections were held before the leader of the opposition announced his scheme.

And since then, the people of Manitoba are still more in favour of the alternate scheme. The hon. member iMr. Logan) has spoken of a union between Mr. MACPHERSON.
the Grand Trunk Railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific. Yes ; there is a very close union between these two companies, but there is also a very wide separation between them. Wherever any benefit is to be got out of the country these two companies are one and indivisable, but where-ever there is any responsibility to be borne they are as far asunder as the poles. United they are, for benefits ; separated when it comes to share responsibility. That is what we object to. The Grand Trunk Railway Company has not hitherto proven itself much of a friend to Canada, and if it is to reap all these benefits which the government seem anxious to shower on it, let it assume the responsibilities and obligations which should accompany such benefits. I cannot understand why gentlemen opposite refuse to impose these obligations on the Grand Trunk. Do they fear the Grand Trunk ? Are they under the control of the Grand Trunk ? Has the Grand Trunk such influence over the government that the government is afraid to impose obligations commensurate to the benefits which they bestow ? Is it, that the mighty shadow which the member for Colchester spoke of, forced itself into the council chamber, and so scared the government out of their wits, that they are afraid to impose any obligations whatever on the Grand Trunk ? That is what the country will ask. These gentlemen opposite, in their newly-found patriotism proclaim themselves the friends of Canada. They forget that one prominent member of the government was howling for secession in Nova Scotia, while other members of the government were advocating commercial union with the United States. The people will not forget these things. These gentlemen in their new found patriotism profess to be desirous that every pound of freight shall be carried over Canadian soil to Canadian ports. If that is not mere hypocrisy intended to delude the people of Canada, why do they not surround this contract with the safeguards that will carry out that object ?
I remember reading of an old coloured man who was out in a heavy thunderstorm when the night was very dark
Chestnuts.

I will attend to you presently. The coloured man was much afraid, and lie prayed : Good Lord, give us less thunder and more light. The hon. gentleman from King's (Mr. Fowler) might have given us less thunder and more light. One of the members from Toronto, spoke of the Grand Trunk Pacific routing its traffic through Chicago, but the hon. gentleman failed to give us the name of any line which is running from Winnipeg to Chicago, or in the direction of the boundary. As a fact, the only road running in that direction at present, is the Canadian Northern Railway,

juicl the Manitoba government entered into a bargain with that road with the object of getting its freight carried to Canadian ports, so that I imagine it would be difficult for the Grand Trunk Pacific to arrange to have Its freight carried to the United States by that railroad. Another member from Toronto repeated the saime argument, but he failed to tell us what distance the railway haul was by that route, or how, when they got the freight to Chicago, they would take it to an ocean port. If there is anything in the argument to which lion, gentlemen opposite have treated this House during the last three or four weeks, that it is an impossibility to take grain by rail over long distances, it should be equally impossible to take it around by Chicago through the State of Michigan and the province of Ontario and on down to Portland. So that if they are right in the one instance, they must be wrong in the other. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition had a proposition of his own before the country, involving running powers, and so on. We do not hear anything about that now. But one part of that proposition was to help the Grand Trunk Pacific to build a road from Winnipeg to the Pacific coast. To show the value of the arguments of hon. gentlemen opposite, one of the hon. gentleman's lieutenants from the lower provinces, the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell), this afternoon said that we need not have given anything to get a road built on the prairie *section because we could have got the Canadian Pacific Company to build it for nothing. It seems to me that that hon. gentleman was turning down his leader, who said he would assist the Grand Trunk Pacific to build through that section of country. If he would, that road would be just as liable to pick up the traffic and take it out by Chicago as the road provided for by this Bill. So that, under the proposition of the hon. leader of the opposition, if it were earned out, matters would be just the same in that respect as they are under the proposition before the House. I do not understand how these hon. gentlemen can advance such arguments. The Grand Trunk Pacific Company are bound by a certain contract to ship all goods to Canadian ports at equal rates to those charged to American ports. The company are liable for the acts of their officials, and if the officials were to do anything else, they would violate the contract. To say that some one is going to whisper into the ears of the officials, and that the officials are going to whisper into the ears of the farmers of the North-west, as to what they should do in this matter, is absurd.. Imagine any railway official whispering into the ear of a farmer and suggesting to him the way he should ship his freight. I know something about station agents in the North-west, and something about farmers. If any railway station agent were to suggest to a farmer how
he should ship his wheat, the farmer would tell him to mind his own business. It seems to me that hon. gentlemen opposite underrate the intelligence of the farmers of the North-west, when they suppose that they would be taken by the ear by railway agents in that way. As a matter of fact, these hon. gentlemen are putting up a man of straw for the purpose of knocking him down. They are doing this, I fancy, for the purpose of taking up time and keeping us here. That may be all very well for gentlemen who can go home on Friday night, and come back on Monday and Tuesday ; but it is not very well for men who live 2,000 miles away.
Amendment negatived on division.

Before the section is adopted, I have one more amendment, which is not very different from the one I last moved. It is to this effect :
Notwithstanding anything in this Act, or in the said agreement contained, His Majesty the King, acting as aforesaid, shall not he bound or obliged to perform, .carry out or fulfil any of the covenants, conditions or stipulations in the said agreement contained on behalf of the Dominion of Canada unless and until the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall have entered into an agreement with His Majesty the King, acting as aforesaid, hy which the said Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall covenant and agree as follows :-
That the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall mot in any matter within its power directly or indirectly permit, advise or encourage the transportation of traffic by routes or at rates other than as provided in the said agreement, and shall in all respects and in good faith use its utmost endeavours to fulfil the conditions upon which public aid is granted and accepted, namely, the development of trade through Canadian channels and through Canadian ports.
I want to say a very few words witb regard to this amendment. The distinction between it and the amendments which I have previously moved, as. my hon. friend the Minister of Justice will of course have observed, is that in this amendment I am requiring that the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall covenant on behalf of itself only, and not on behalf of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. In other respects, it is exactly the same as the other amendment. I have gone Into this matter fully in connection with the last amendment, and I need not make any extended observations. Bet me say, in reply to my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan), that he' is not making this matter any clearer by speaking as he does of these corporations. He say that If we regard them as one institution, the Grand Trunk Railway must be bound. Well, an argument of that kind would sound fairly well perhaps out of the mouth of a layman, but my hon.. friend is a member of the bar of some experience, aud surely be will not, In the presence of law. yers, commit himself to the proposition that

the Grand Trunk Railway is liable under any stipulation in this contract, merely by the fact that it holds a controlling Interest in the stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. I understood him to say that the Grand Trunk Railway is really bound because the two corporations are the one institution.
My hon. friend is mistaken. I said nothing of the kind.
Then he does not pretend that the Grand Trunk Railway is bound by any stipulation in that contract?
I am not making that contention.

I thought he would not dare, as a lawyer, to make it. Well, the object of the last amendment is that the Grand Trunk Railway shall be bound by one of the most important stipulations in the contract, namely, that the trade shall not be diverted from Canadian ports. My hon. friend from Saskatchewan (Mr. Scott), said that my alternative proposition the other day permitted exactly the same difficulty which I am trying to guard against here. He forgot, no doubt, that when I made my proposition the other day, I expressly said that in giving aid to the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway in the west, I would exact from the Grand Trunk Railway in that regard exactly the same stipulations as we were exacting from the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. In proposing this amendment, I am carrying out exactly what I said. I have eliminated from this amendment any obligation on the part of the Grand Trunk Railway to become responsible for the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, and I am asking that the Grand Trunk Railway, so far as its own acts are concerned, shall undertake that it will not, directly or indirectly, permit, advise, or encourage the transportation of traffic by routes other than those provided in this agreement, and shall in all respects and in good faith use its utmost endeavours to fulfil the conditions upon which public aid is granted and accepted, namely, the development of trade through' Canadian channels and through Canadian ocean ports. Whatever objection there may have been to the previous amendment, in so far as it asks the Grand Trunk Railway to covenant for the acts of another railway company, is removed by the form of this amendment, which merely requires the Grand Trunk Railway to covenant that it will not divert traffic from Canadian routes, but will in good faith use its best endeavours to fulfil the conditions of the agreement.

By his first amendment, my hon. friend proposed that this Grand Trunk Railway should guarantee all the obligations of the Grand Mr. BORDEN (Halifax.)
Trunk Pacific Railway under the contract. Then he proposed his other amendment that neither the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway nor the Grand Trunk Railway shall permit or advise or encourage the transportation of traffic by routes or at rates other than as provided in the agreement. Then comes the last amendment, which practically is the same, the only difference being that the Grand Trunk Railway simply covenants on its own behalf. The same argument that applied against the other amendments also applies against this, and I need not repeat them.

Mr. Chairman, I have an amendment which I wish to move to this clause. I move:
That section 8 of the Bill be amended by addling thereto the following .-
Provided that the said railway, in its course through the province of Quebec, shall run from the Quebec bridge, on the River St. Lawrence, in a south-easterly direction through i.ho counties of Levis and Dorchester, following the course of the Etchemin river up towards Etche-min lake and thence easterly through the province of Quebec towards the city of Moncton.
In regard to the proposal to construct this railway, I may say that I do not believe that the Prime Minister, in his speech on the 30th of July last, in introducing this Bill, explained exactly what he intended to say in regard to the location of this railway. The Prime Minister stated that the railway would run through the counties of LGvis, Bellechasse, Montmagny L'ls-let, ICamouraska and Temiseouata. I do not know whether he did it intentionally or accidentally, but nevertheless he did not mention the county of Dorchester, and indirectly the First Minister said that, owing to the chain of moontains, the line would have to run south of the range of mountains. I may tell the right hon. Prime Minister that in running a railway from the Quebec bridge easterly, in order to secure a crossing of the mountains at the proper place, lie would have to run it through the county of Dorchester. You will hear in mind that in the province of Quebec there are only two rivers which cross the Alleghany mountains, the Champlain or Richelieu river is one and the other is the Etchemin river. These are the only two rivers in the province of Quebec that flow from the south through the Alleghany mountains and into the St. Lawrence river. Consequently, this is a natural pass for a railway. If you go into the library you will see that the first l-ailway that was
run in 1837 h-om Levis to St. John, N.B., was run right through that valley. I have myself, as a boy, heard my father talk about that, and he showed me some of the stakes that marked the place where the engineers had mil their line. Hon. gentlemen will bear in mind that the stretch of land between the state of Maine anid the St. Lawrence river varies in width from about 30 to 45 miles, and in length it is about 110 miles. In running a railway from the north-west corner of that belt of land to the south-east, it would be impossible to run it in a straight and direct line, because to do so you would have to run your road lengthwise through the Alleghany mountains. I have read five or six reports, and they all show that it is almost impossible on account of the heavy grades and sharp curves. The result is that you will have to build the railway at an angle. If you do not make your angle at the west end, you can run down along the Intercolonial to Riviere du Loup and then make your angle at the east end, going towards Edmundston. If you don't make your angle there, you have to make it through the county of Dorchester.
Now, as I said, that line varies from 30 to 45 miles. Those six counties are well served already by the St. Lawrence and by the Intercolonial. The Intercolonial runs Horn about one mile to six miles from the St. Lawrence. The north side of the mountains has been settled up for a great many years. The jteople who live on the north side of the mountains do not need the railway at present, and probably never will need more railway facilities than they have now. So you have between the Intercolonial and the boundary line of the State of Maine, a belt of land only 28 to 40 miles wide. By building this new road where I suggest the government should buildi it, on the south side of the mountains, you would build it at the very place where it is needed. That part of the country I know very well. The people have a pretty hard time to live there. It is a well timbered country, but they can only sell their timber to the people in Maine. Their timber has to he floated down the St. John river, and they get very small prices for it generally. They have no other way of shipping their timber except down the River St. John. But by running this railway where I am suggesting, you would serve all these counties very satisfactorily. The route I speak of and the route recommended by the government both start from the bridge at Chaudi^re, as I find by this map prepared! by the government. I compare this map with one issued by the Quebec government, and I find by them that both roads start at the Chaudiere bridge and run probably 50 miles from one to five miles apart, and in the county of LYslet they join and become one road. That is about ail the difference there is between the two routes. One route up to the Etchemin river

is tlie natural route; the other was surveyed by a. man named Tache, whom 1 know very well. It goes up the Etchemin river to a place called Itiver Abenalds, and then it takes a very heavy grade for about eight ibiles. In fact it follows a zig-zig course all the way through the mountains ; sometimes it runs east and sometimes west, and sometimes north. Well, Sir, the line I propose to the government is the best that could be discovered. You can run that line thirty miles from the Chaudiere bridge without a curve, or a cut, or a fill, or a bridge. I say now plainly to the government that from the ChandiSre bridge for about 45 miles, if they find it necessary to build a bridge over 20 feet long, let them call on me and I will build the bridge myself. Moreover, I have this to say to the government, if you have any desire to build a road through there let me know before you send engineers, and I will show them the route and I will not charge the government one cent for my services. I could show them 45 miles in about four days.
Now the other day the bon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) read a statement made by an engineer named Light. That report from Mr. Light was a pretty fair one, it was made in 1884 or 3885, when the conditions were not such as they are to-day. He was instructed to start at St. Anselme, and he kept on the east side of the Etchemin river and encountered some awful curves, and some awful cuts. But to-day, owing to the Quebec bridge being under construction, the whole matter is changed. The departing point and the arriving point of the railways must be at the Quebec bridge. That changes the situation altogether. That is the only reason why I move this amendment asking the government to run the road through the county of Dorchester, and in doing so it will run also through all the counties named by my hon. friend.

I am very glad that my hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Morin) has changed his rniud with regard to this Bill, and he now sees there is some merit in it. That is a disposition which I think he did not indulge at a former stage of the discussion. At all events, it is never too late to repent and to amend one's ways, and I congratulate my hon. friend that he has seen new light in favour of this enterprise. With regard to the amendment he offers, he will agree with me that it would be premature to localize the road at the present time. I stated when introducing this Bill that I thought the line would start from the Quebec bridge and go south of the range of mountains. In that case I hope it will pass through the county of Dorchester, it must pass inevitably through the county of Levis, and I think it will also pass through Dorchester and some other counties there. But he will agree with me that Mr. MORIN.
it would be impossible at the present time to say that the road must pass through any particular locality. That is a question for the engineers to decide.

My right bon. friend tries to put me in a false position. But I will tell him frankly, while we are looking at each other face to face, that if there is any one to blame because I did not support this scheme at first, it is my hon. friend the leader of the government-and you know who he is, no doubt. As I said before, I do not know whether it was intentionally or accidentally, but in naming the counties through which the road was to pass the right lion, gentleman left out the county of Dorchester. Soon after, my hon. friend the Minister of Justice spoke to me about it, and I replied to him, If you give me nothing you get nothing from me. I may say this much to the Minister of Justice and to the First Minister, that if you attempt to run a line through there, try and get an engineer who is an honest man, and I assure you that he will run that line where I am asking you to run it. But If you get a Vanderbilt engineer or a Hays engineer, well, I do not know where he will run the line.
Amendment (Mr. Morin) negatived.

Mr. Chairman, I desire to move an amendment to section 8 as follows :
That 'section 8 of Bill (No. 235) intituled an Act respecting the construction of a National Transcontinental Railway be amended by striking out the worlds ' city of Moncton ' in the second line thereof and inserting in lieu thereof * the town of Truro via Parrsiborough, Five Islands and Great Village ' and that the contract in the schedule of the said Act De varied accordingly.
In the course of this debate the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan), whom I am glad to see here, was good enough to inform us that the reason that the road stopped at Moncton was that from there could radiate a number of lines to different parts of Nova Scotia. He was good enough to say that Mr. Hays had said that there would he not only freight enough for one port to handle but freight enough for five or six ports to handle and that therefore from Moncton might radiate other railways to different ports in the maritime provinces. 1 understand that the reason that this railway is left at Moncton is that every hon. gentlemen from the maritime provinces may go to his constituency and claim that the ocean port is to be in his county. I noticed a short time ago that Mr. McDonald, of Pictou, after coming here, went home and intimated to the press in his county that he expected to have an ocean port at Pictou by a line along the north shore of my county, perhaps, and his county. I am delighted that the province of Nova Scotia at least is to he so generously treated that it is not going to have one ocean port hut

many. The hon. member for Cumberland, in exploiting this splendid eventuality, undertook to say that very likely the road
would	be	extended	into	my county,because	the	line in	its	course eastwards	first	passes	into	Cumberland,
then into Colchester and then through to Halifax. We have been agitating for a railway to be built through my county for a long time from Truro along the shore of the Bay of Fundy by way of Economy and Five Islands to Parrsboro', and thence connecting with the Intercolonial Railway near Amherst. When the Intercolonial Railway was built it was thrown 15 to 20 miles back from the shore. Hon. gentlemen frequently talk about parallel lines and the necessity of having railways within a short distance of each other. Last summer at a meeting which was held in my county to discuss this question one man got up and said : My farm, which I received from my father 30 years ago, was worth at that time $12,000, but I could not get more than $2,000 for it now because I am on the Bay of Fundy, and by the Intercolonial Railway being built away from the Bay of Fundy the whole of the trade has been taken back and we are side-tracked. Therefore, there has arisen in the county of Colchester an agitation to have a railway from Truro to Parrsboro' which would follow the course of the old highway in connecting with Amherst and thus avoid the Cobequid mountains. When the Intercolonial Railway was built it was taken over the Cobequid mountains and of course this increased the grades of the road. The grades are too great for a great ocean to ocean railway. Not only are the grades too great but the curvatures are greater than would be permissible on a transcontinental road. When the Intercolonial Railway was located the notions we have of railways to-day were not in existence. People believed that if they had a railway it was a railway no matter what course it took, just as people in the olden time believed that an ordinary road which crossed a mountain was just as good as one that went around it. The Intercolonial Railway was located with many curves. When it left Truro it was swept away from its proper course in order to meet the requirements of the Acadian iron district thus making the Grecian bend. After going to the Londonderry mines it had to be pulled away in another direction in order to get through the Cobequid mountains by way of the pass. The pass is a very high one and although it crosses the Cobequid mountains it makes an enormous grade to surmount. After it crosses the Cobequid mountains it is pulled again to the west to get to the Springhill mimes. Therefore, the Intercolonial Railway is a zig-zag route located to meet the then local requirements of the country and iu consequence of that is not fitted in any way to be a transcontinental railway. At
tlie time that the Intercolonial Railway was surveyed the route that I propose, from Truro along the shore of the Bay of Fundy by way of Economy and Five Islands to Parrsboro' was surveyed, and these surveys are in the railway department. That route was recommended as the proper route for the Intercolonial Railway but the political forces of that time backed by the capital of the country determined to take it by this other route which probably better suited the business interests of the country then. I am not complaining about the location of the railway. The line was put there in the best interests of the country at that time,
I presume, but now, since we are going to have a transcontinental line which requires grades and curves such as the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) has spoken of, I desire that the railway shall follow the approved route from Moncton to Truro along a level line without grades and with very few curves. My hon. friend from Cumberland county was kind enough to suggest to me that when the Grand Trunk Pacific was built and connected with the Intercolonial Railway at Moncton a single line between Halifax and Moncton would be unable to handle all the business. We would have to double track the railway, and as the hon. gentleman said before, we would, in double tracking the Intercolonial Railway, be duplicating and perpetuating its grades and curves. He said we had better swing it around by Parrsboro ' and Truro, and get a better road. I fancied he had some quiet understanding with some gentleman in my county, who might be my opponent next election.
Possibly.

I have no quarrel with any of my colleagues in the maritime provinces, but I noticed the extreme generosity in the proposition, in that, when his own county needs so many railways, he should be so kind as to make this offer to my county which has so few. I therefore thought, that when such an offer had been made, it might be misunderstood during the election if I did not say something here. My training has been a business one, and if there is any possible way of making an arrangement so as to have no misunderstanding, I would adopt that way. I therefore ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Logan), and the Prime Minister, and the Minister of Finance, to give us a helping hand, and without any further ado here or on the hustings let us have the terminus of this line at Truro. There will be this great advantage. Moncton is ISO miles away from an ocean port. You can not even smell the salt water at Moncton, but when you come to Truro you are only C>2 miles away, and the shad that are fished out of Halifax harbour at three in the morning are delivered on our breakfast tables.
And lobsters.

And sharks.
Mr. GOL'RLEY. Anyway we have the smell of the salt water at Truro which they have not at Moncton. I want this railway to have some of the appearance of a salt water railway, and consequently I hope the the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance will give me a helping hand.
A salt water railway is something new.

Of course, I mean a salt water port. 1 move this, hoping that my friend (Mr. Logan) who has been so kind, will now get his friends on the other side to support it, and I will have great pleasure in telegraphing to Truro in the morning that: We have been selected as the ocean port instead of Moncton.
I will guarantee that the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Gourley) will not be supported by many of his own party.
Oh, yes.

If the hon. gentleman desires, we will take the vote and test it. I do not think that this amendment is a serious one, and therefore I shall not waste the time of the House about it. The facts are : We determined that any transcontinental railway should he built into the maritime provinces, and with the conflicting interests of the different ports, we had to settle upon some one point as a compromise. We found that we could all agree on the city of Moncton, and Moncton was incorporated in the Grand Trunk Bill as the terminus and it was supported by my hon. friend (Mr. Gourley). He did not move such an amendment as this to the Grand Trunk Bill, when it was on its passage through this House, and it is too late for him now to think of it. I have no doubt that when this road is built to Moncton, and when the words of Mr. Hays come true, that there is enough traffic for half a dozen ports, we will not only have a government railway built from Maccan or Athol, around by Parrsboro', and Five islands to Truro, but we will also have a road built from Moncton, through northern Westmoreland and Cumberland counties, and on to Pictou, to connect with Sydney, Country harbour, Louisburg and Whitehaven ; thus accomplishing a saving in distance of 39 miles between Moncton and New Glasgow. These are things that are bound to come. However, we have entered into an agreement that Moncton should be the terminus in the maritime provinces, and that was incorporated in the Grand Trank Pacific Bill. I believe myself that a road will be built south of the Cobequid mountains to accommodate the traffic, but it will be built by the government itself as part of the Intercolonial Railway. There is a great temptation to-night for a member on this side of the House to speak at some Mr. LOGAN.
length, because if we ever had an opportunity of holding these gentlemen opposite tip to ridicule, we have it now. They talk about paralleling the Intercolonial Railway, hut here is a proposition from their side, by which, the hon. member for Colchester proposes they will have two ra il-ways running side by side and paralleling the Intercolonial Railway from Moncton to Maccan or Athol.
With a branch to Amherst.

My hon. friend is not acquainted with the geography of that country. He could not branch off at Amherst. These lines would be running side by side according to his proposition, until we could divert the line at Maccan or Athol, probably, to Parrsboro' and on to Truro. These gentlemen opposite have talked about the Intercolonial Railway as being the pet lamb of Canada. But the hon. gentleman (Mr. Gourley) now talks about the zig-zagging of the Intercolonial Railway, and the Grecian bend on the Intercolonial Railway and the bad grades on the Intercolonial Railway, and he winds up by saying that it is useless as a transcontinental railway, crossing as it does the Cobequid mountains. The temptation is great to retort on these gentlemen opposite, but I think the country understands their position.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Logan) is very good to refrain from obeying the calls of temptation. It shows a strong virile nature, and I congratulate him. But, when a man is not weighing every word he utters, he says very funny things. The hon. gentleman says ' we ' have entered into an agreement to adopt the city of Moncton as the terminus. Who are ' we ' ? As a member of this House, I have not entered into any agreement, and I do not think my friends on this side have. Who are ' we ' that undertake silently and secretly, behind the backs of their fellow members to enter into this agreement ?
I will tell my hon. friend who are 'we.' 'We' include the member for Colchester who voted for this resolution in the Railway Committee.
My hon. friend is incorrect. I was in Nova Scotia when that resolution was passed.
Will my hon. friend deny that he supported the resolution to build to Moncton ?

I have not supported any resolution yet. I have been reluctantly compelled to vote against the government project because I wanted a transcontinental scheme, if it were a wise one. And, if the friends of a transcontinental railway are driven to oppose this scheme, what on earth will be the attitude of those who are

opposed on principle to the building of any transcontinental railway? My hon. friend from Cumberland cannot exploit against me any attempts to belittle any of the insti-tions of Canada. I have endeavored to maintain them throughout my whole life, and have never said anything against them. Therefore, it is idle for him to attempt to exploit anything against me in that regard. Although the Intercolonial Railway has bad grades, it was located in the business interest of Nova Scotia. But our ideas of what a railway should be were entirely different then from what they are now. We then thought that a railway to connect two points was all that was needed. We know now that a railway means the most direct route between two points, with the easiest grades and the fewest curves, and equipped with the most complete rolling stocks. Local railways may continue to have grades, but railways intended to compete for transcontinental traffic must have practically no grades. I am a student of the geography of this country. I believe we possess in Canada the strategic position with regard to the trade routes of this continent, and that through this continent we command the trade routes of the world. The people of Canada are rather slow to apprehend these new ideas, but I have no doubt that in ten years every man in Canada will realize the truth of what I am now saying. I think this debate marks an era in the history of Canada. It is the only great debate that has occurred in the parliament of Canada. You could have thrown half the other debates into the sen, and you would have improved the literature and the political history of Canada. This debate is worth all the others put together. From this time we will know the geography of the country better than before, and lie more intelligent men. I suppose the hon. member for Cumberland thought that I should take the offer of his kindness for the thing itself. I know that it is not right to look a gift horse in the month, and perhaps I should have regarded his offer as a young and pretty colt, although it had the appearance of an old nag, knock-kneed and maimed, and intended to be exploited at the next election in Colchester. My hon. friend appeared in my county before the last election. I may say that he is known to have a splendid lot of kites, and I understand that his friends telegraphed to him : ' Come over, Logan, and bring your best kites.' And he did appear with the finest assortment of kites that I ever beheld, and I have no doubt that he gave his political friends some aid by the exhibition of those kites, and one of them was to build the very road which we are now talking about. He had met all the leading men in the county of Cumberland, and they were all prepared to build this railway through my county. That was only four or five days before the election, and the greatest sorrow the hon. gentleman had was, that
they had not given him more notice. If they had, the railway would have been built by the time of the election. The most he could do was to assure them that the road would certainly be built. I tried to tell tlie people that this gentleman was a kite-flyer and did not mean half what he said. They said, it is impossible that this gentleman, with his sincerity of manner, does not mean everything he says, and they took his kites as realities. Was it the Trojans who feared the Greeks bearing gifts ? 1 fear the hon. gentleman bearing the gift of this great transcontinental railway to my county. I want him to get his friends to support the resolution that Truro is to lie actually the winter port. We do not want any more kites. They look very nice in the air, but they are not railways. Surely, ray lion, friends will vote to extend the road from Moncton to Truro, a distance of only sixty-two miles from the ocean. With that extension, there will be a very good transcontinental road from Truro to Halifax. If we do not get this port at Truro, I am going to appeal to the Finance Minister to give us a subsidy of $10,000 a mile for a railway from Truro to Five Islands, though I would much prefer to have this transcontinental railway. I would be delighted to have the road pass through my county, and I hope all hon. gentlemen will vote to have the ocean port located there.
I would call the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that his own leader has gone out, and is not here to vote.

I wish to say just a word with reference to the amendment submitted by the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Gourley). In answer to the remarks made by my hon. friend, I would say that while I appreciate his motives in asking for a road from Moncton to Truro, I would be opposed to such a road being built to parallel and sidetrack the present Intercolonial Railway. But if it Is to be a part of the Intercolonial, it would in that case be in the interests of the public generally, and it would shorten the distance between Moncton and Truro by some fifty miles. That is, take the road from Moncton to Sackville. which could be made a straight line, and from Sackville to the mines, south of the Cobequid mountains, and you would have an easier road with better gradients and less curvatures, and shorten the distance as expressed. With an object of that kind, I would readily support the amendment as submitted by the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Gourley), but I would stoutly oppose having the line a part of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, to parallel the Intercolonial Railway.
Amendment negatived.

I am not sure whether the question I want to raise comes under this section. In this agreement I do not see anv reference to the operation of telegraph

lines. Whether this omission he intentional or not, there is no doubt that telegraph lines in connection with the eastern section and also in connection with the western section, should belong to the railway company and the earnings form part of its revenue. There should he no loop hole allowing a separate company to be organized for the operation of these lines. It is well known that the telegraph business in connection with such a railway system could not fail to be an exceedingly valuable asset. It would be operated at very little cost and bring in a very large revenue. I feel quite sure the government will agree that there ought to be some clause providing that the telegraph lines should belong to the railway company and not be diverted to another company and the profit therefrom be taken from the railway company.

Under section 22 of the charter provision is made for the construction of telegraph and telephone lines along the railway, and also that the company may construct and operate the lines for its own profit. But as regards the eastern division, section 22 would not apply. The suggestion is one worthy of consideration. It would, however, have to be dealt with in a special clause and I will undertake to do that.
Mr. Obl.EIt. No doubt it is within the knowledge of every one in this House that the question of telegraph monopoly, both in Canada and in the United States, has been a very serious one. When the telegraph companies were first making very large strides, it was quite natural that they should make agreements with railway companies to use their poles, and obtained monopolies for twenty-one years or longer. These monopolies were frequently of enormous value. In the case of the Western Union Company, I think that the privileges which it obtained from the various railway companies, especially the transcontinental railways, were of such value that the stock of the company was watered to the extent of $30,000,000 or $40,000,000, and yet the earnings were sufficient to pay the dividends and interest. Within the last five or six years the railway companies have been trying to shake off these monopolies. In the ease of the Baltimore and Ohio, they have succeeded, but the Pennsylvania Railway Company have had many law suits over old agreements >in connection with branch lines which they had acquired. In the present case, assuming that this road is to be a transcontinental one. the telegraph franchise in connection with it will be of great value, worth millions of dollars, and it is very important that a careful arrangement should be made to prevent any control of the telegTaph system passing into the hands of any private company. It would be legitimate for a private company to lease a line from the Grand Trunk Pacific
Railway in the west and then from the government in the east, and in that way get an enormously valuable franchise, which ought to go to swell the revenues of the eastern and western portion, and I am quite sure that this arrangement would meet with the approval of every member of this House and with the approval of the country.

I think that matter would have to be considered altogether independently of section 8. My horn, friend Mr. Osier) has not overlooked the fact that so far as the western end of the line, the section from Winnipeg to the coast is concerned, clause 22 of the charter provides that the company may construct, control and operate telegraph and telephone lines. The question to be considered would be in reference to the eastern extension, from Winnipeg. Provision has been made for the operation of telegraph lines, but it is exclusively for the operation of the road. If it is intended to use that telegraph line for the purpose of general business we would have to make a special provision for it. It is not contemplated in the present agreement.

It would be a very simple matter to string an extra wire along these poles, a very small thing compared with the *value of such a service. I am not finding fault in any way but in looking over this clause it struck me that it would be as good a clause as any on which to bring up this matter. I am not pressing it at all.
A special clause would be necessary and I will see that a section is drafted'.

Section agreed to.
On section 14,
I thought that the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Toronto was to section 17, but apparently from the record of the chairman it must have been moved to section 16.
Perhaps it would be better to bring this up when we come to consider section 2. This amendment has reference to the question of customs duties with respect to the contract.

If my hon. friend would have no objection to having section 10 stand it would1 perhaps be better. I have prepared an amendment to the section but I am not quite convinced yet whether it will be necessary to move it.
Section allowed to stand.
On section 19, member of parliament not to be paid employee or contractor.
Would that refer to what is called .a silent partner, a party who is interested but whose name would not appear ? That is a common way of evading

tire law and I would like to know whether this would coyer such a case ?
The MINISTER O'F JUSTICE. Certainly it would, if any attempt to evade the law in that way was made the parties could easily be reached under the Independence of Parliament Act. This is the best I could do in the way of drafting a clause but I am quite willing to accept any amendment that would better meet the object desired, that is to prevent any member of the Senate or of the House of Commons having anything to do with this matter directly or indirectly for profit. I have adopted this clause from the Intercolonial Act. It is practically the same section as in tbe Intercolonial Railway Act and I think it is similar to the Independence of Parliament Act, but if we can improve it and make it more effective, I am willing to consider any suggestion.

I am not saying it would not be effective, but I think the way such laws have been evaded before is by means of construction companies. A tender would be put in and a contract obtained but names of the parties interested would not appear ; but they would be silent partners all the same.

I think this clause stood the other evening on account of some discussion with respect to the general question of the independence of parliament. The Minister of Justice will recollect that we discussed the possible necessity of some amendment to that Act by reason of the fact that so many of the business transactions of the country are carried on at the present time by corporations. The Prime Minister said that some discussion had arisen some twenty years ago, and that no better safeguards could be found than those which we now have in the Independence of Parliament Act. I think I mentioned at that time, that very many of the commercial transactions of the country, nearly all of the business transactions of the country, are carried on now by persons associated together under the form of corporations, and somewhat different considerations might apply now to those which applied twenty years ago. I think we discussed the possibility that, notwithstanding the clause the Minister of Justice has taken from the Act respecting the construction of the Intercolonial, it would be possible for the members of the Senate and House of Commons to associate themselves together, to go through the necessary form which would constitute them a joint stock corporation, and to make any contract with the commissioners, which means a contract with the Crown, that they might see fit. It seems to me, the Minister of Justice permitted this clause to stand at that time for the purpose of considering whether the government could offer to the House any addition to the words to be found here which 378
would obviate what might be a difficult situation in that regard. It is quite true, that under modern methods you could have members of parliament contracting with the Crown in respect to this large enterprise, under the guise of a corporation. I am not using the word ' guise ' in any offensive sense, because it would he quite proper for gentlemen to do that, as the law stands at present-at least, it would be quite legal. Now, the Act respecting the Independence of Parliament has not taken that change of condition into consideration. It may be necessary that at a very early date we should take that change of conditions into consideration. But we are dealing here in this contract with interests that may run up to 50, 75, 100 or even 125 millions, according to the various estimates which have been made of the cost of this undertaking. When you go into a business of that magnitude, is it not time to consider whether you should not have some better safeguard than is to be found in the general Act relating to the Independence of Parliament ? We have got along, it may be said, fairly well, without any great scandal up to the present time. At least it has not come within my knowledge that members of parliament have associated themselves in the form of a corporation for the purpose of contracting with the Crown. But it might also be said that no such temptations as would be presented by a scheme of that kind have up to the present time made themselves felt. When you are here, face to face with an undertaking of this magnitude, is there not fair room for consideraton as to whether, in respect of this enterprise, some other safeguard should be provided which would prevent members of parliament from taking the course I have suggested they might take, a course which may be taken by members with perfect propriety under the Act respecting the Independence of Parliament.

The section 11 provides :
This Act shall not extend to disqualify any person as a member of the House of Commons by reason of his being a shareholder in any incorporated company having a contract or agreement with the government of Canada.
That is the general principle; here is the important exception :
Excepting any company which undertakes a contract for the building of any public work.
No member of parliament can be a shareholder in any company which undertakes to contract to build any public work. We might have to amend section 15 to read as foliows :-
No member of either House of parliament shall receive an appointment to any office of emolument under the commissioners, or shall be a contractor or party to any contract with the commissioners, for the construction of the said eastern division or any part thereof, and the said eastern division shall he declared for



the purposes of this section a public work within the meaning of section 15.
That is to say, we declare this to be a public work, and, as a result, it will be impossible for any member of parliament to be a member of any incorporated company which is in any way connected with this enterprise. It appears, therefore, to be quite clear, that no member of either House of parliament can be a stockholder in an incorporated company which would undertake a contract for the building of any public work in connection with this enterprise.

Would it not do to add at the end of the third line the following:-
No member of either House of parliament shall hold or be appointed to any office of emolument under the commissioners, or shall be a contractor or a party to any contract, either Individually or as a member of any incorporated company, with the commissioners for the construction of said eastern division.
That is to the same effect. Either suggestion would meet the case.

I think the Minister of Justice suggested the other night that a company might be formed for the purpose of furnishing supplies. I do not know whether that would be important enough to require us to deal with it. There is one more suggestion which occurs to me, from examining section 15, that is, whether the same form that was adopted then with regard to the Canadian Pacific Railway should not he adopted now with regard to the western division of this railway.
I can see no objection to that.
The expression in this statute is, ' any company incorporated for the construction of any part of the Canadian Pacific Railway.'

I have no doubt it will be a public work for the purposes of this Act.
supplies. This opens up rather a large question. You might have a man in business for instance a large hardware merchant who would be in a position to furnish hardware supplies. Are you going to prevent the commissioners or a contractor from purchasing from that gentleman in the open market ? It seems to me that it would be very far-reaching if that is the intention of the hon. gentleman. I would like to understand what is intended, because, when one is expected to draft anything, it is necessary for him to know what the object is that is aimed at. If my hon. friend would say that he would be content that we should make section 15 of the Independence of Parliament Act applicable to this road in its entirety, to both the eastern and the western divisions, it is very easy for us to do it, but if it is intended to go beyond that and to make the prohibition applicable to all those who might have occasion to furnish supplies to any contractor, I do not know where it is going to lead us.

I think it is going to be a very difficult thing, because in a case of the steel company, for instance, its shareholders are all over the country. Any one having a few shares of stock would be absolutely precluded from furnishing supplies. It would be a very desirable thing to do in some ways, but at the same time it is very difficult to frame a provision that would exactly meet the case.

If these parties were furnishing supplies direct for the government they would come under the disqualification. The only doubt would be in case they tshould furnish supplies to a contractor. We could hardly go as ar as that.

I will endeavour to have drafted in my department a clause upon the lines of section 15 of the Independence of Parliament Act, and if there is any suggestion to offer in addition to that we will consider it.
However, if the hon. Minister of Justice will prepare some such amendment as he thinks will meet the case we can then consider it.

As far as the individual is concerned I do not imagine that we can add anything to the clause which is here. It is only where a member of parliament might be a member of an incorporated company that there is any question.

I understand that this amendment should be made applicable to the western division and that divison should be put in the same position as a public work within the meaning of section 15. I understand that to be the extent to which my boil, friend would desire that we should go in respect to the furnishing of Hon. Mr. FITZPATRICK.

Will the hon. gentleman consider the question of equipment as well as supplies ? The equipment of this road is a very large item, amounting to some $20,000,000, and while I see some very great difficulty in applying the law to ordinary supplies, it might be very important that members of parliament should not deal in matters that might involve many millions.
That would be a direct contract, and there would be disqualification in that event.

That
would be a contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific.
I only suggest that the hon. member should consider the question.
That would come under the section, because that would he a contract in respect to the equipment of the road, and it would be a violation of the spirit of the clause.
It might not be a public work.
Still, the equipment is part of the road, is it not 5 If we declare the road to be a public work, of course, the equipment, it seems to me, would become a public work as a matter of necessity.

I think the language would probably require to be a little closer than that contained in section 15. The language is ' any company which undertakes a contract for the building of any public work.' Of course, the building of different portions of this work might be undertaken by a great many different companies or contractors, Then, as far as supplies are concerned, really the only thing I (had in my mind was a company formed for the purpose of furnishing supplies-
To contractors ?
No, to the commissioners.

What I was seeking to guard against waf members of parliament forming themselves into a company for the purpose of furnishing supplies to this railway whether to contractors or to the commissioners. That is an entirely different thing from the furnishing of supplies by a merchant, or by a going concern at the present time.

As between the commissioners and persons 'furnishing supplies they would clearly be disqualified, because the commissioners stand in place of the government. But, suppose a contractor takes a contract from the commissioners and becomes a perfectly independent person, is he to be prevented from buying his hardware at the shop of a member of parliament ?

No, the only prohibition would be against members of parliament, now or in the future, associating themselves together in the form of a corporation for the purpose of furnishing supplies for the building of the road whether to contractors or to commissioners. That is to say, looking at the worst possible aspect of the case, we might have a number of members of parliament forming themselves into a corporation for the purpose of furnishing supplies to contractors and relying upon their political influence to see that the contractors bought from them. Although that is a very remote contingency, it should be guarded against.

Well, I am content to leave it in the judgment of the hon. Minister of Justce.

On section 21-power to suspend work.
Does the hon. Minister of Justice remember why we allowed this section to stand ?

It was considered that perhaps it would be inadvisable to put such a great power in the hands of the government. We thought that by adopting this section, we were reserving to parliament control over the whole work. If there is any objection to that, we are not wedded to it at all. We are quite willing to let it go. I myself adopted it from the Intercolonial Railway Act, and from the Quebec, Montreal, Ottawa and Occidental Railway Act.

The only difficulty I see in the clause is that it leaves it in the hands of the government to stop the work until the next session of parliament. In the meantime, if the surveyors or engineers report against the work, and if the Grand Trunk Pacific are anxious to get out the contract to operate the eastern portion of the road, the government might take that means of abandoning it entirely.

That can be done without suspending the progress of the work. Supposing that during the progress of the work, we met with some unforeseen difficulties, is it not proper that parliament should have some control over that ? I would like to have the views of my colleagues on the subject, but so far as I am concerned, I do not think there is anything to be gained by keeping the clause in, beyond giving parliament absolute control over the enterprise.
You have absolute control over a government work at any time.

There is nothing in the clause beyond the possibility that something may arise that we have not clearly in our mind now. Suppose we should come to the conclusion that the commissioners were not properly discharging their duties-which is not at all likely to happen with the excellent commissioners that will be chosen-but suppose it did happen, and we did not wish to act at once, we merely say that we will reserve our judgment until parliament meets. We

attach so little importance to the clause, that if anybody has grave objection to it, we do not insist on it staying in.
If its scope is what the Minister of Justice suggests, there is no objection to it, so far as I can see at present.
I may confess that it was taken bodily out of the Intercolonial Railway Act.
That is the usual clause in the Public Works Act.
It practically is. The Minister of Justice might consider whether it is not desirable to incorporate it.
Suppose we pass the clause, and then if later on it is considered advisable to add the amendment, we can consider it.
There is no objection to that.
